headline: IND/EX 2026: Big Theatre Chains Have Customers. Independent Cinemas Have Communities. - Celluloid Junkie
summary_text: As consolidation, shifting release windows and funding pressure reshape the film business, IND/EX 2026 showed independent exhibitors and festivals organizing around community value, operational resilience and a stronger collective voice. ... While much of the global exhibition business gathered in Barcelona for CineEurope, independent cinema operators, art house leaders and film festival allies from across North America met in Chicago for a very different kind of industry conversation. ... Organized in partnership, and in something close to spiritual kinship, by Art House Convergence (AHC) and Film Festival Alliance (FFA), IND/EX 2026 brought together the independent exhibition and festival communities for four days of “community education, networking, and industry advancement.” Presented by marquee sponsor Filmbot, the event marked the partners’ second Independent Film Exhibition Conference, following the inaugural edition in 2024 and a standalone Art House Convergence meeting last year. ... This year’s event drew 788 registered delegates, up from 728 in 2024, and reflected a sector increasingly focused not only on programming and audience development, but also on sustainability, advocacy, accessibility, staffing, funding and the role independent cinemas play in their communities. ... CineEurope often speaks in the language of investment, technology and market share, IND/EX frequently spoke ... the language of care: empathy, safety, ... , labor, accountability and enrichment. ... of this made the gathering any less ... For Stuart, that approach includes listening to the community, keeping prices accessible and treating the cinema as more than a place to sell tickets. During the pandemic, Stuart Cinema & Café was declared an “essential” resource hub by the Governor, after supporting neighborhood residents in ways that included giving away leftover food and helping facilitate virtual viewings of burials across the country. ... The Numbers Behind Independent Cinema’s ResilienceThe latest audience data presented at IND/EX suggests that Stuart’s point is more than anecdotal. ... Feedback collected from more than 27,000 moviegoers for Art House Convergence found that more than 70% of respondents say their preferred art house destination is “very” or “extremely valuable” to their overall quality of life. Meanwhile, 91% agree that their theatre “elevates the experience of being in this community.” ... “Independent theatres show impressive revenue-generating horsepower,” Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends at Rentrak, noted. “Put into circuit terms, they would collectively represent the 13th largest grossing group of cinemas year-to-date in the United States. Independent cinemas that are part of Art House Convergence have seen an 8.8% uptick in year-over-year grosses, and an impressive 38% over 2019.” ... The survey also showed that respondents attend more than 10 films annually at their preferred art houses, which represents 55% of their overall moviegoing habit. While that figure has remained steady over the last two years, art houses continue to attract new and younger guests. Nearly a quarter of respondents, 24. ... %, first began attending their preferred art house within the last three years. Their average age is 40, compared with the overall respondent average of 51, and 68% of recent attendees are younger than 45. ... “Art house cinemas are vital gathering spaces, and an essential component of today’s independent film ecosystem,” Lela Meadow-Conner, AHC’s interim executive director, remarked during the presentation of the results. “Our latest survey proves that audiences continue to rally around their local independent theatres, and despite current challenges, like shifting theatrical windows, media consolidation and arts funding pressure, moviegoer support for art houses continues to grow.” ... Film festival attendance is also showing signs of durable growth. Eventive, the independent film ticketing and streaming provider and an IND/EX sponsor, shared five years of sales data covering 15 million tickets since 2020. According to the company, the “post-COVID bounce” has settled into a higher baseline for the sector, defined by deeper engagement. ... Average revenue per ticket climbed to its highest level yet, exceeding USD $13 in 2025, while capacity utilization has consistently surpassed pre-pandemic benchmarks, averaging in the mid-50% range. ... “Audiences are not merely returning; they are placing a higher value on the shared cinematic experience than ever before,” Iddo Patt, Eventive’s co-founder and CEO, stated. “Whether it’s at the movie theatre and in-person events, virtual screenings, or the intelligent application of new technology, our common goal remains the same: bringing people together around the power of film.” ... Haj, who also served as the first vice president of FFA at its founding, said the partnership between independent cinemas, festivals and distributors has become increasingly important at a time when independent distributors remain under pressure. ... “When we see independent distributors under pressure, getting bought and disappearing, it is incredibly important to bring them closer to the cinemas,” Haj urged. “We must work to shorten the distance between the cinema and the independent filmmaker, who may or may not have distribution.” ... Haj also emphasized the need for independent cinemas and festivals to speak with a more unified voice, particularly as the broader media and entertainment business continues to consolidate. Government officials, she argued, often understand the for-profit theatrical model better than they understand independent cinema. ... “Those big chains, they have customers,” Haj stated. “We have communities. That’s who we are.” ... That distinction, she suggested, matters when policymakers are considering issues that affect film access, repertory programming, independent distribution and the future shape of the film ecosystem. ... The more AHC and FFA members contribute to their organizations, Haj encouraged her colleagues, the better those organizations can advocate on behalf of the sector. “We need more movies, not fewer. We need more partner companies, not less. Corporate mergers do not help the public.” ... Karen Cardarelli, president of the FFA board and executive director of Facets Film Forum in Chicago, made a similar case for continued collaboration. ... “When festivals and cinemas unite, our influence rises, our advocacy strengthens, and our collective voice becomes impossible to ignore,” Cardarelli noted during her opening night remarks. “Not long ago, many of us were wondering what the future of our organizations was going to be. But today, we are not just celebrating a recovery. We are celebrating a remarkable comeback.” ... For independent cinemas and festivals, IND/EX 2026 was not simply a conference about survival. It was a signal that the sector is increasingly organizing around a broader proposition: community is not just the emotional value independent cinemas provide. It may also be their strongest business argument. ... /EX 2026: Big Theatre Chains Have Customers. Independent Cinemas Have Communities.- July 12, 2026

On June 13, hundreds of true believers gathered at the Alex Theatre in Glendale, California dressed in colorful, reflective, space-age outfits to watch a film and celebrate the existence of aliens. They weren’t there to watch Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day” but “Welcome Space Brothers,” a documentary about the Unarian movement and their benevolent leader who believed she communed with extraterrestrial life, Ruth Norman. ... The movie has played film festivals since 2023, but absent any real distribution, the producers, alongside Elijah Wood’s SpectreVision, took it upon themselves to release the film whichever way they could. June 13 was the beginning of a roadshow on behalf of the film in which director Jodi Wille plans to tour to at least 15 different cities, do Q&As, and engage with local followers of Norman’s teachings. The Alex Theatre screening also featured a live performance from rocker Moby, who is a co-executive producer on “Welcome Space Brothers” and via his production banner Little Walnut bankrolled the film’s P&A to make this tour happen. ... Wille is not a household name, and Moby will not be performing at other tour dates. But the initial screening netted $8,500 in profits, and the team at SpectreVision is confident the film will find its audience even in communities like Boise, ID, Roswell, NM, and more places that aren’t New York or LA. ... Campagnola, who co-heads SpectreVision’s Management division, told IndieWire. “One person came up to me after the screening and was like, ‘This film is going to usher us into the Age of Aquarius!’ I love that so much. It just takes on a life beyond the film, and it’s really about finding like-minded people that share the same weird beliefs you have. The question is how do we continue to do this for other movies? It has to be a ... SpectreVision is just one indie shingle experimenting with the roadshow method of release, staging individual screenings of the film and making each into an event featuring the film’s stars, subjects, or filmmakers. Even distributor Utopia and their boutique label Circle Collective, which has released far more music docs for which the roadshow makes perfect sense, is touring around director Greg Vrotsos and his film “Situations” to make sure it doesn’t disappear on streaming. ... It’s hardly a new idea, but it’s rapidly becoming more prevalent a method for independent releases, as well as for traditional distributors trying to shake things up. Filmmakers and production companies are looking at the traditional means of distribution and believe something is broken. ... “Look at some of the box office. It’s insane. Something runs an entire week and does $600. That doesn’t make any sense to keep that movie for a week,” said Jessica Rosner, an independent distributor and theater booker currently working on a roadshow for the film “The Last Picture Shows.” “If you do know your audience, if you’re able to target your audience, you’ll get them there to those one or two shows, and it’s better for the theater.” ... Rosner is one of the masterminds behind the roadshow for “Hundreds of Beavers,” which looks like the template everyone wants to copy. The black-and-white, slapstick silent comedy made for just $150,000 became a cult hit surpassing over $1 million in box office after launching a tour of the film around the Midwest, not the coasts. ... To this day, it continues to play one-off screenings nationwide, many of them involving appearances with costumed beavers from the film. Rosner clarifies it wasn’t the Midwest tour that secured the movie its New York and LA dates, but it did spark the word of mouth that drove more people to it. ... In the case of “Welcome Space Brothers,” the film has people who belong to a literal cult who are now coming out to watch it. “The Last Picture Shows” is a documentary about independent movie theaters past and present, and Rosner and distributor Gary Rubin are taking it directly to those offbeat theaters the movie is profiling. ... Karol Martesko-Fenster of distributor Abramorama said the roadshow’s popularity for indies is emblematic of our “direct-to-audience” era. Rather than blanket your movie across the country and try and drum up attention through national press and marketing, filmmakers are appealing directly to theaters with a pitch for why their movie can perform there by packing the house on a single night, selling them on Q&As that can help make the screening more of an event. They’re tapping into local news outlets to drum up attention and then doing hyper-targeted marketing through social media using zip codes to make sure the right audience finds the title and is willing to go out for this one-night only event. ... All of this requires massive coordination and effort on the part of the distributors — sometimes handled by the filmmakers themselves— to not just do the marketing but also geographically map out a tour schedule where a filmmaker can reasonably get to day-to-day. You also have to navigate exhibitor schedules if a date doesn’t work or if they have studio commitments that bar them from screening another title, and Rosner explains that you may literally not have the luxury of booking numerous screenings in advance. ... Martesko-Fenster shouted out Sam Green’s “32 Sounds,” an experimental film that needed to be seen in a theater and wound up having Green touring around in a station wagon for a full calendar year on behalf of the film. Martesko-Fenster said it was that effort that got the attention of the Criterion Channel to eventually place the film on streaming. ... “This is really where the work of a distributor comes into play,” Martesko-Fenster said, “The roadshow is more work, but they’re open to it because there’s a financial return that’s better, and there’s an awareness return that is much better, because you’re able to get regional PR to compliment national PR, and you’re able to get pockets of supporters to interact with the filmmakers.” ... Campagnola with SpectreVision — which itself is not a distributor — is literally doing the outreach to these arthouse theaters herself, and she and her partner at the company believe artist-led distribution is the future. If they can raise the P&A budget, is there a means in which all the profits can go back to the filmmakers? ... That requires tracking down audience data that can literally be a black box, and it’s a huge burden on anyone to be a creative and a data scientist or marketing executive, Campagnola said. But it’s incumbent on distributors in whatever format these movies are released to begin asking those questions. ... “A lot of them don’t ask the filmmakers, ‘Where do you think your audience lives?’ The filmmaker’s involvement is crucial because they would know where the touch points are. Identifying those keywords and finding the audience is an important first step,” she said. “I don’t want to come across as bashing traditional distribution, but obviously the system is broken. It’s not a surprise to anyone. I know they’re trying to figure it out, but a lot of times they’re trying to satisfy an international, 100-screen deal. That’s what’s always baffled me. If a filmmaker knows they can sell out a theater in Glendale, California, why wouldn’t you book that theater?”

So the answer is no, I had no idea I would ever own a movie theater,” Stevenson said in an interview Friday evening, along with Manager Josh Vazquez. Stevenson, his wife and their six children moved here for Stevenson to work at Maple Leaf Farms, which ended up being a temporary job. At one point in 2024, he wanted to open a trampoline park at the former Marsh building on South Buffalo Street, but that didn’t work out. “So that idea of entertainment and fun, that’s been in my bones ever since I was a kid,” Stevenson said. “But I’ve been working in corporate America for 15 years or so.” As for his background, he graduated in organizational psychology, business psychology, statistics and surveys. After moving here and the job didn’t work out, he started hunting for opportunities. “We definitely want to stay here. I have six kids. So then when the opportunity came up (to buy the theater), I was actually talking to Nicodemus Cards, he’s a close neighbor of mine, and he mentioned that it was on sale so I just kind of pursued it, thinking that it would be wild and crazy, but when I saw the numbers I saw potential. I saw some community engagement and marketing opportunities. I saw it as a legitimate business,” Stevenson explained. Bess Joyner, the original owner of North Pointe Cinemas, died in November 2024, Vazquez said. Around that time, the family decided to put things up for sale, he stated. “It’s been a wild ride. It’s been work,” Stevenson said. While Stevenson said he doesn’t have the experience yet of operating a movie theater, Vazquez does. “He makes it all work. Him and his team. He’s been in the industry for 25 years. I was like, ‘This is stupid. I can’t do any of this.’ But once I met him, within 4 minutes, I knew this is a people operation. I know people. I can do the marketing. Josh knows everything about this business, and so that’s kind of been the key there. He knows what he’s doing,” Stevenson said. Vazquez said he started “slinging popcorn” in Anderson when he was 16 for Goodrich Quality Theatres. At 18, Vazquez became a projection manager. He read all the manuals and learned everything he could about film and projectors. At 20, he was running the theater. In 2008, they built the Hamilton 16 IMAX in Noblesville, and that became the No. 1 movie theater in Indiana and top 200 in the nation. After that, Vazquez worked for Goodrich in Lebanon, Ind., and Brownsburg. He then started traveling around to the various theaters for Goodrich. In 2020, Covid happened, Goodrich filed bankruptcy and had to liquidate everything. The Joyners reached out to Vazquez and offered him the manager position that had become open. He took a chance, uprooted his family and moved to take the job in Warsaw. “Since then, it has not been an easy journey, trying to get back. We were very fortunate that a good amount of the community understands how important it is to try to maintain having a cinema in Warsaw. Those people come in and buy concessions. They understand that there’s some things we can control, and some things we can’t. The way the contracts are with the studios and everything, concessions are how we pay our kids. So, supporting the concession stand is really the big thing that was able to make it to where we were able to survive,” Vazquez said. They were able to get the Shuttered Venues Operating Grant, which he said was probably the theater’s saving grace during 2022-24. The Hollywood writer’s strike caused problems for the theater when it was happening. “So we’re slowly getting out of that,” Vazquez said. Water Incident Back in April, North Pointe Cinemas had a water main break, which caused the business to be closed for a couple weeks. Showing where the “water incident” happened, Vazquez said, “Right here is where the main line actually coming in broke.” The room where it occurred was being used for storage. “Essentially, this 8-inch main line broke underneath the ground and ended up just shooting up water up into this area. Hit the bottom of the concrete. Hit the vapor barrier and the styrofoam, and then just went to all the walls and just started shooting up. My shift manager described it, when I was on the phone with her, she said it looked like the Titanic.” A lot of dirt and material were pushed up against the edges of the walls. The floor heaved a little bit. Vazquez said there was a lot of water and it’s crazy how much damage water can do. “Even with 2,500 gallons of soda on the floor, it still heaved about an inch in this room,” he said. Stevenson said it’s been fixed and the space is livable, though they still have work to do to that room where the water incident started. The carpet in the building is still to be replaced. “So the carpet and the walls, we decided, obviously, keeping up our numbers is a big thing for maintaining both people staying, used to going to the movies - since Covid that’s been a big thing we’ve been trying to overcome, is how do we get people back into the movie theatres?” Vazquez said. “Because since Covid, we still, even in year 2026, we get people coming in saying, ‘This is my first time going to a movie since 2015, 2017, 2018.’ Then they get out here and they’re like, ‘I forgot how much this experience is just better than sitting at home on the couch and having to pause the movie every five minutes while one of your kids goes to the bathroom.’” Stevenson said going to a movie at the theater is an experience. Wanting people to continue coming out to movies, Vazquez said they’ll catch up to the repairs in August when school is back in session and the work can be completed during the morning hours. “It was important for us to try to get back open for the community, both because the community was literally calling us every single day, ‘When are you guys opening? When are you open? We don’t want to go anywhere else,’” Vazquez recalled. Stevenson said there was also a lot of misinformation about the theater being spread, too, as people started noticing the “for sale” signs popping up as well. He said they were three months into the deal of him buying North Pointe Cinemas when the water incident happened. Vazquez pointed out there also was no fire, despite the rumors. No one died. The theater didn’t close because it was being sold. Planning Ahead “The goal has been to, how do we take the cinema in this area to the next level?” Vazquez said. “Both with our customer service, with staying competitive with our pricing and then really just trying to figure out a way to improve that experience, but not at the detriment of keeping the business open and whatnot.” Stevenson said it seems like the consumer base is the secret to that. “Understanding how much they want, and how much they’re OK with, to make not only a profitable business, but something that feels new and refreshing,” he said. While Vazquez said they would love to do things like reserved seating and reclining seats, “On the ‘Endgames,’ on the ‘Doomsdays,’ on these big titles where you really need as much capacity as possible ... you lose half your seats when you do recliners.” The cost used to be $200,000 per auditorium to switch over to recliners, he recalled. summary_text: Backed by Maersk and ₹1 ... , India challenges China ... # Backed by Maersk and ₹10,000 crore, India challenges China’s 95% monopoly ... ## India has built its first EXIM-grade container for a global shipping line. Backed by Maersk and a ₹10,000 crore government scheme, it now wants to break into a market dominated by China. ... Nearly every good you've bought that arrived by sea travelled inside a steel box built almost entirely in one country. Chinese manufacturers produce more than 95% of the world's dry cargo containers and close to 100% of refrigerated ones, according to shipping consultancy Drewry. The dominance is so complete that in May 2026 the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment against four Chinese container makers and seven executives for allegedly running a price-fixing cartel that roughly doubled prices between 2019 and 2021. On July 3, 2026, India quietly tried to open a crack in that monopoly. ... Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal unveiled the first export-import (EXIM) grade container manufactured in India for an international shipping line, at the Maersk-CONCOR Inland Container Depot in Dadri, Uttar Pradesh. It was built by DCM Shriram Group, better known for fertilisers, sugar, and chemicals than steel boxes, for A.P. Moller-Maersk, the world's second-largest shipping line. ... The "first" needs an asterisk. India has had container capacity before, including Jupiter Wagons' Indore plant. What's new is a box certified to EXIM grade and accepted into a global carrier's fleet, a much higher bar than one that never leaves the country. ... Maersk ordering 1,000 more India-made containers immediately after the unveiling moves a supplier from prototype to procurement. Small by global standards, where carriers buy tens of thousands a year, but meaningful as a first repeat purchase. ... Maersk has history here. In September 2021 it agreed to sell Maersk Container Industry, its refrigerated container arm, to CIMC for $987 million. That was an exit from manufacturing, not a bid for independence. It collapsed in August 2022 after the DOJ's Antitrust Division concluded it would consolidate over 90% of the world's insulated and refrigerated container production in Chinese state-owned or state-controlled hands. ... The DOJ never formally sued; the parties abandoned it once it was clear it wouldn't survive merger review. It would have combined two of only four global reefer suppliers, which tells you how thin the market is. ... China's grip didn't happen by accident. It followed a familiar pattern, first US-dominated, then Japan, then South Korea, which by the 1980s built more than 70% of the world's containers, before Chinese scale, cheap steel, and state support made competing elsewhere unworkable. CIMC alone accounts for roughly 42% to 45% of global production, with Dong Fang and CXIC taking most of the rest. ... The barrier is cost, not physics. A 40-foot container costs roughly ₹1.5-2 lakh to build in China against ₹3.5-4 lakh in India. Some of that is logistics, since an empty box built far from an export market must be repositioned before it earns anything. Most is unit economics: steel prices, line throughput, and the amortisation of plants running at millions of TEUs a year. That's why the subsidy design matters as much as the ribbon-cutting. ... The Union Budget 2026 allocated ₹10,000 crore over five years to a container manufacturing scheme, called the Container Manufacturing Assistance Scheme in budget documents and the Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme by the shipping ministry. It aims to lift annual capacity tenfold, to 7.5 lakh TEUs, through capital support for new plants, operating support to bridge the cost gap, and R&D funding. The groundwork traces to a February 2025 meeting between Prime Minister Modi and Maersk's Robert Maersk Uggla. ... India isn't the first challenger. Vietnam's Hoa Phat, which built a container plant beside its own Vung Tau steel mill, delivered 1,000 twenty-foot boxes to CMA CGM in August 2025 and runs 200,000 TEU a year of a designed 500,000. That cuts both ways. The monopoly is contestable, and contesting it takes captive steel, proximity to an export market, and patience. ... Containers are infrastructure so ubiquitous it's invisible, the physical unit global trade is measured, priced, and moved in. A country that can't build them depends on whoever does, price-fixing and all. One box won't dent China's dominance, and the real test is whether DCM Shriram can deliver repeat quality at a cost that survives the withdrawal of subsidy. But it's a genuine entry into a market with almost no alternatives for over a decade, and a reminder that the most consequential manufacturing stories aren't always about flashy products. Sometimes they're about finally building the boring box everything else travels inside.

headline: India breaks into China's steel box monopoly after costly lesson - The Economic Times
summary_text: India has launched its first export-import (EXIM) shipping container for global deployment, marking its entry into a sector overwhelmingly dominated by China, which controls about 90-97% of global container manufacturing. ... For decades, India has quietly relied on a product that is so basic to global trade that most people rarely notice it. The steel shipping container powers trade of everything from engineering goods to electronics, yet almost every steel box used by Indian trade comes from China.India has just taken a symbolic but significant step towards changing that reality with the rollout of its first export-import shipping container manufactured for global deployment. The move marks the beginning of an ambitious effort to enter an industry where China's dominance has remained virtually unchallenged for decades.ALSO READ | Maersk places order for 1,000 shipping containers with DCM Shriram Group ... Few manufacturing sectors are as concentrated as container production. China accounts for close to 90-97 per cent of global container manufacturing capacity, depending on the segment and year. The dominance is so complete that shipping lines, exporters and logistics companies across the world have little choice but to source containers from Chinese factories.India's dependence on these imports was not merely a commercial issue. It reflected the absence of a domestic ecosystem capable of producing containers at scale and at globally competitive prices. While India emerged as one of the world's largest trading nations, it lacked meaningful capacity to manufacture the very steel boxes that move much of international trade. That imbalance became increasingly uncomfortable as geopolitical tensions rose and supply chains became more vulnerable to disruptions. ... The push for container manufacturing in India can be traced directly to the pandemic years. As global trade patterns were disrupted, containers accumulated in some regions while becoming scarce in others. Exporters struggled to secure boxes. Freight rates surged and supply chains became unpredictable. Indian exporters and importers felt the impact sharply. The shortage highlighted the risks of depending on a single country for a critical piece of trade infrastructure. ... What had previously been viewed as a low-priority manufacturing segment suddenly acquired strategic significance. Policymakers began looking at container manufacturing not simply as another industrial activity but as an element of supply-chain security. ... The concern extended beyond Covid. Policymakers and industry executives increasingly worried that any future geopolitical conflict, trade dispute or major disruption involving China could once again leave India exposed. ... The government's response gathered pace over the past two years. Container manufacturing was identified as one of the strategic sectors that India wants to develop under its broader manufacturing push. The biggest policy intervention came in the Union Budget this year, which announced a Rs 10,000 crore Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme. The objective is to create a globally competitive domestic ecosystem rather than merely establish a few isolated factories.The scheme proposes capital support for new manufacturing facilities, assistance for expansion of existing units and operational support to bridge the cost disadvantage faced by Indian manufacturers. It also includes provisions for research, testing, skilling and technology development. The government expects the initiative to increase domestic manufacturing capacity dramatically over the coming years and create the foundation for a viable industry. ... Building containers may appear straightforward, but competing with China is another matter. Industry executives estimate that containers manufactured in India currently cost 30-40 per cent more than those produced in China. In many cases, the difference can be around $700-1,000 per container. Chinese manufacturers operate massive, highly automated facilities that benefit from economies of scale developed over decades. They also enjoy deep supply chains for steel, components and specialised equipment.Indian manufacturers are only beginning the journey. Land costs, smaller production runs and the absence of large-scale automation make it difficult to match Chinese prices. The challenge is not merely about producing containers. It is about producing them consistently, efficiently and at a cost that global shipping lines are willing to pay. ... The latest milestone would likely not have happened without the active involvement of global shipping giant AP Moller-Maersk. The company worked with DCM Shriram Group to develop prototype EXIM containers built to its specifications. Teams from Denmark and independent auditors evaluated Indian manufacturing capabilities and inspected facilities before the project moved ahead.The unveiling of the first India-manufactured EXIM container at Dadri in Uttar Pradesh last week represents an international validation of India's ability to meet global quality and safety standards. Maersk's decision to place an additional order for 1,000 containers is even more important. The order provides commercial credibility to India's emerging manufacturing effort and offers local producers the scale needed to improve capabilities and lower costs.India is caughgt in a classic chicken-and-egg problem. Large orders are needed to achieve efficiency, but efficiency is needed to attract large orders. Maersk's intervention helps break that cycle. ... Reducing dependence on imported China-made containers is the most obvious benefit, but it is far from the only one. A domestic container industry creates demand for steel, fabrication, welding, coatings, logistics services and specialised components. It encourages the development of ancillary industries such as corner castings, flooring systems and container paints. The government estimates that the sector could generate substantial direct and indirect employment while creating a market worth tens of thousands of crores over the next decade.The initiative also aligns with India's wider maritime ambitions. The country is investing heavily in ports, shipping infrastructure, shipbuilding and logistics networks. Container manufacturing fills an important gap within that broader ecosystem. For a country seeking to become a major manufacturing and export hub, ensuring reliable access to containers is increasingly viewed as a strategic necessity rather than a simple procurement issue. ... India's entry into container manufacturing remains at a very early stage. China retains overwhelming advantages in scale, technology, supply chains and cost competitiveness. No one in the industry expects that dominance to disappear anytime soon. Yet the significance of India's first globally certified EXIM container lies in what it represents. The country has moved from discussing the problem to producing a market-ready product for one of the world's largest shipping lines.Whether India ultimately becomes a major container manufacturing hub will depend on how quickly manufacturers can narrow the cost gap, improve productivity and secure sustained orders from global shipping companies. The journey could be difficult but after years of complete dependence on imported containers, India has finally taken its first meaningful step into one of the most strategically important segments of global trade.

India has emerged as one of the fastest-growing packaging markets globally, expanding at a steady pace of around 9% annually to reach $92 billion by FY30.1 Demand is being driven by food processing, pharmaceuticals, personal care, and the rapid rise of e-commerce, which alone has introduced new packaging intensity per order. Per capita packaging consumption in India remains significantly lower than global averages, indicating strong headroom for growth. ... Yet, the significance of this expansion lies in how packaging is being repositioned. It is no longer limited to protecting goods. It now plays a role in branding, customer experience, and, most critically, operational efficiency. As supply chains become more formalised and geographically dispersed, packaging must adapt to more complex distribution requirements. ... India’s logistics sector, currently valued at USD9B in FY25,2 is undergoing rapid transformation with large-scale investments in warehousing, industrial corridors, and multimodal connectivity. The development of Grade A warehousing alone has expanded significantly in the past few years, particularly across key consumption hubs such as Mumbai, NCR, Taloja MIDC, Navi Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Chennai. ... Modern facilities are larger, more structured, and increasingly mechanised. Conveyor systems, automated sorting lines, and forklift-based handling require packaging formats that are standardised and compatible with machine-led movement. This shift has led to a move away from irregular packaging towards uniform, stackable units that can move seamlessly through different nodes of the supply chain. The objective is clear: reduce manual handling, improve throughput, and minimise transit damage. With logistics costs in India still estimated at around 7.97% of GDP,3 efficiency gains from better packaging integration are becoming a strategic priority. ... While primary packaging continues to influence consumer perception, the real operational gains are being driven by secondary and tertiary packaging. These layers determine how efficiently goods are stored, transported, and delivered. Transit packaging has become a strategic consideration, especially for industries operating at scale. It directly impacts loading time, warehouse space utilisation, and damage rates during transit. Even marginal improvements in these areas can translate into significant cost savings across high-volume supply chains. ... The rise of quick commerce and same-day delivery models has further intensified the need for robust transit packaging. Products are expected to move faster through the system, often within tightly compressed timelines, leaving little room for inefficiencies. ... At the centre of this transition is palletisation. The ability to move goods in consolidated units has transformed warehouse operations and transport efficiency. Instead of handling individual cartons, entire loads can be lifted, stacked, and transported in a single movement. Within this system, wooden pallets continue to play a defining role. India’s pallet market is expanding in line with logistics growth, supported by increased adoption across FMCG, retail, pharmaceuticals, and manufacturing sectors. A significant share of this demand continues to be met by wood, given its availability and cost advantage. ... Wooden pallets, sourced from responsibly managed forests and backed by PEFC certification (PEFC/42-31-06), remain widely used due to their structural strength, adaptability across industries, and ability to handle heavy loads. They are compatible with existing warehouse infrastructure and can be easily customised for different use cases. In a country where supply chains must accommodate a wide range of product types and transport conditions, this flexibility is critical. Their relevance becomes even more pronounced in high-volume sectors. Pallets act as the base unit of movement, ensuring stability during transit and enabling efficient storage within warehouses. Without this layer, the speed and scale at which goods move across the country would be significantly constrained. ... Another factor driving their continued use is lifecycle flexibility. Wooden pallets can be repaired, refurbished, and reused multiple times, extending their operational value. This has led to the emergence of organised pallet recycling and refurbishment networks, reducing overall material costs while supporting sustainability goals. ... As interdependencies between packaging and logistics deepen, businesses are moving towards integrated solutions. The focus is shifting from sourcing individual components to designing systems that improve overall supply chain efficiency. ... This includes customised transit packaging, pallet pooling, repair services, and material optimisation strategies. Providers operating in this space are aligning closely with industry requirements, offering solutions that improve handling efficiency without adding complexity to operations. The emphasis is on enabling smoother movement of goods while maintaining consistency across different stages of the supply chain. In many cases, the effectiveness of logistics infrastructure depends on how well these packaging systems are designed and implemented. ... India’s packaging expansion reflects a bigger structural change in the economy. As consumption grows and supply chains become more sophisticated, the role of packaging is being redefined. The real momentum lies in the integration between packaging formats and logistics infrastructure. Warehouses, transport networks, and material handling systems are no longer independent elements. They function as a coordinated ecosystem, with packaging serving as the interface connecting them. ... Wooden pallets, often overlooked in broader industry discussions, sit at the core of this system. They enable scale, support efficiency, and provide the physical foundation on which modern logistics operates. As the sector continues to expand, the competitive edge will come from how effectively companies align packaging decisions with logistics realities. In that alignment lies the true engine of India’s packaging growth.

The Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR), Government of India, has issued its final findings dated June 25, 2026, in the anti-dumping investigation concerning imports of Virgin Multi-Layer Paperboard originating in or exported from Indonesia. Concluding that dumped imports from Indonesia have caused material injury to the domestic industry, the Authority has recommended the imposition of anti-dumping duty ranging from USD 261 per metric tonne (MT) to USD 376 per MT for a period of five years. ... The investigation was initiated following an application filed by the Indian Paper Manufacturer Association (IPMA) on behalf of the domestic industry. The participating domestic producers included Aditya Birla Real Estate Limited (formerly Century Textiles and Industries Limited), Emami Paper Mills Limited, JK Paper Limited, ITC Limited, and Tamil Nadu Newsprint and Papers Limited (TNPL). The period of investigation covered April 1, 2024, to March 31, 2025, while the injury assessment examined data from 2021-22 through the investigation period. ... According to the final findings, the product under consideration is Virgin Multi-Layer Paperboard made solely from white or virgin wood pulp, whether coated or uncoated. The scope includes Folding Box Board (FBB), Solid Bleached Sulfate Board (SBS), Cup Stock Paper or Board, and Liquid Packaging Board (LPB) in the range of 140 GSM to 450 GSM. The Authority excluded paperboards manufactured using recycled or brown pulp, coated or uncoated cigarette boards, two-side coated artboard imported for printing purposes, and four or more layered paperboards used in liquid packaging applications. ... A key issue during the investigation was whether SBS and LPB should be excluded from the scope. Interested parties argued that these grades were not imported from Indonesia during the investigation period and differed from other product categories. However, the Authority rejected the request, noting that the domestic industry manufactures and supplies SBS and LPB and that the same machinery and production processes can be used to manufacture these grades. The Authority observed that there was no justification for excluding these products merely because imports were not recorded during the period of investigation. ... The Authority further noted that Virgin Multi-Layer Paperboard is primarily imported under Customs Tariff headings 4805 and 4810, although imports have also been reported under multiple other tariff classifications. ... Several interested parties contended that the existing Minimum Import Price (MIP) mechanism already addressed any injury caused by imports and that anti-dumping duty would result in overlapping protection. They argued that the MIP effectively neutralized price undercutting and therefore fulfilled the objective of trade remedial measures. ... The domestic industry, however, maintained that the MIP is only a temporary measure and does not eliminate dumping. According to the industry, the MIP merely establishes a floor price and remains below the cost of sales of domestic producers. The industry also argued that injury margins remained significant even when the MIP was considered as the import price. ... The Authority agreed with the domestic industry's position, observing that the MIP remains temporary in nature and is valid only up to September 30, 2026. It concluded that the existence of the MIP neither eliminates dumping nor removes the need for anti-dumping duties. The Authority further found that imports at MIP levels could still cause injury to the domestic industry. ... Regarding injury and causal link, interested parties argued that imports from Indonesia accounted for only 4.24% market share during the investigation period and therefore could not be considered a significant cause of injury. They also pointed to imports from China and Chile as a major source of competitive pressure on domestic producers. ... The domestic industry countered that imports from Indonesia had increased sharply during the investigation period due to low-priced offerings by Indonesian exporters. It stated that while imports from China and Chile exerted pressure in earlier years, Indonesian imports became a significant factor during the investigation period, forcing domestic producers to lower prices below their cost of sales. ... The Authority found that import volumes from Indonesia increased dramatically from just 108 MT in 2021-22 to 61,567 MT during the period of investigation. After examining all known factors, including demand trends, productivity, technology changes, consumption patterns, and imports from other countries, the Authority concluded that dumped imports from Indonesia had caused material injury to the domestic industry. headline: Extended Producer Responsibility In India: Assessing The Progress Of The Circular Economy Transition
summary_text: As India’s economy grows, managing waste is becoming more difficult. Urbanisation, higher consumption, greater e-commerce, and the increased use of electronics have changed the amount and type of waste produced. Plastic packaging, e-waste, and used batteries are growing quickly, creating environmental and health problems that traditional waste systems can’t keep up with. ... In the past decade, India has increasingly incorporated EPR into regulations for plastic packaging, electronic waste, and batteries. Over the last ten years, India has added EPR rules for plastic packaging, e-waste, and batteries. These changes have reshaped how the country manages waste, aiming to make producers more accountable, boost recycling, and protect natural resources. Still, it’s worth asking: Is EPR really speeding up India’s move to a circular economy, or is it just making small improvements in waste management? ... The Plastic Waste Management Rules, which began in 2016 and were later updated, established one of India’s first major EPR systems. These rules require producers, importers, and brand owners to collect and process plastic packaging waste from their products. The challenge is huge. ... At first glance, a recycling rate of almost 60 % looks good. But 1.65 million tonnes of plastic still escape formal recycling. For every three kilograms of plastic used, about one kilogram still ends up in landfills, is burned in the open, or leaks into nature. Our important concern is the growth in plastic consumption itself. Per-capita plastic waste generation increased from approximately 700 grams in 2016-17 to more than 2.5 kilograms by 2020. This suggests that while recycling capacity is improving, waste generation is expanding rapidly, creating a moving target for policymakers and recyclers alike. ... A major step forward was the launch of the Central Pollution Control Board’s digital EPR portal and certificate-trading system. Companies can set up their own collection systems or buy EPR certificates from approved recyclers. This market-based system gives companies flexibility and encourages investment in recycling. ... The rise in formal recycling rates is a good sign. In just four years, India’s official recycling rate almost doubled, showing that EPR rules and better recycling systems are starting to make a difference. ... However, these gains must be seen in context. More than half of India’s e-waste is still handled outside the formal system. Almost one million tonnes are processed informally, often in ... Recent E-Waste Management Rules have set stricter collection targets, introduced digital tracking, and made registration mandatory for producers and recyclers. These steps make things more transparent, but their long-term success depends on bringing informal networks into the formal system. (CPCB, 2024) ... One of the most future-focused parts of India’s EPR system is the Battery Waste Management Rules, which started in 2022. ... The timing is significant. India’s electric mobility ambitions are expected to drive battery demand from approximately 4 GWh in 2023 to nearly 139 GWh by 2035. While this transition is critical for decarbonization, it will also generate a substantial volume of spent batteries containing valuable materials such as lithium, cobalt, nickel, and lead. As of 2022, lithium-ion batteries already accounted for about 700,000 tonnes of India’s total 1.6 million tonnes of e-waste. ... Recognising this challenge, the rules establish progressive recovery targets (Government of India, 2022a): ... | Year | Material Recovery Target (Li-ion Batteries) | | --- | --- | | 2024-25 | 70% | | 2025-26 | 80% | | 2026-27 onwards | 90% | ... For EV batteries specifically, collection targets require producers to recover 70 % of batteries placed in the market by 2027–28, and from 2027–28 the rules also require a minimum share of recycled material, starting at 5 % and rising to 20 % by 2030–31. As with the plastics framework, the battery rules rely on a certificate-based system, where producers must meet recycling obligations through registered recyclers. Even here, though, informal recycling is estimated to handle a large share, roughly 80 % by some CPCB-linked estimates, of India’s battery waste, underlining how far formalization still has to go. ... Perhaps the clearest achievement has been the formalization of recycling activity. Before EPR, much of India’s recycling happened informally, with little regulation, oversight, or consistency. The introduction of EPR rules has increased demand for certified recyclers and properly equipped processing facilities. The tradable EPR certificate system, in particular, has created a genuine financial incentive to invest in recycling infrastructure, since certificates themselves now carry market value. ... The rollout of centralized digital portals has made it easier to track what is happening across the system. Producers, recyclers, and waste processors are now required to register and report their activities, which has generated far more reliable data on how much waste is being generated, collected, and recycled. This is a meaningful improvement over the patchy, fragmented reporting that existed before, and it gives regulators a much better basis for monitoring compliance. ... EPR has also encouraged the recovery of materials that can be reused in manufacturing. Recycled plastics, metals from electronics, and materials recovered from batteries are increasingly being fed back into production processes. This reduces the need to extract virgin raw materials and is a direct, tangible step toward the resource efficiency that circular economy thinking is built around. ... This contrast illustrates a broader pattern within India’s circular economy transition, regulatory frameworks are evolving faster than supporting systems. (Kaza et al., 2018; World Bank, 2022) ### ... A significant number of producers, particularly smaller businesses and informal market players, still operate outside the formal EPR system altogether. They avoid registering, avoid reporting, and avoid meeting their obligations, all while their compliant competitors bear the costs of doing things properly. This unevenness not only undermines the overall effectiveness of EPR but also creates an unfair playing field that discourages full participation. ... India’s recycling has long relied on millions of informal waste pickers, aggregators, and scrap dealers. Yet, despite their key role, most EPR systems still operate separately from these informal networks. Leaving out informal workers makes the system less efficient and raises fairness issues, since they have always been important for resource recovery. ... - Strengthen enforcement against non-compliant producers and free riders. - Improve traceability and verification systems to eliminate fraudulent reporting. - Integrate informal waste workers into formal collection and recycling networks. - Expand recycling infrastructure in smaller cities and rural regions. - Encourage manufacturers to adopt eco-design principles. - Increase public awareness regarding waste segregation and responsible disposal. - Create stronger market incentives for the use of recycled materials. ... Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) has become a cornerstone of India’s circular economy transition. Over the past decade, the country has moved from a fragmented, largely city-led waste management system towards one with greater producer accountability, formal recycling markets, and improved resource recovery. ... While significant progress has been made, challenges such as weak enforcement, compliance gaps, inadequate infrastructure, and the limited integration of informal workers continue to hinder its full potential. The next phase must focus on strengthening implementation, improving transparency, expanding recycling infrastructure, and prioritising waste prevention alongside waste management.

This means the sector is preparing not only for the current 40% mandate, but also for the future increase to 60% in 2028-29 recycled content,” Jain clarified. ... Under German rules, commercial goods vehicles weighing more than 7.5 tons and trucks towing trailers are generally prohibited from driving between midnight and 10 p.m. on Sundays and public holidays. ... 'Romanian haulers do not compete in a local market, but on the same routes with Western European carriers. summary_text: EU road freight grows, but cross-trade and cabotage fall | trans.info ... # Eurostat’s 2025 data: international operators lose further ground ... EU road freight grew by 0.9% in 2025, but the headline figure conceals a split market: domestic haulage expanded while the cross-border segments that many carriers depend on for their livelihood continued to shrink. AdobeStock/Gina Sanders ... takeaways - EU road freight rose 0.9% in 2025, reaching 1,886 billion tonne-kilometres - Growth was driven by domestic haulage (+2.2%), while cross-trade (-3.7%) and cabotage (-3.0%) both fell - Poland remained the largest market by tonne-kilometres (381 billion, 20.2% of the EU total), followed by Germany and Spain - Germany featured in six of the EU’s ten busiest freight corridors, led by the Germany-Netherlands route (86.9 million tonnes) ... Transport performed by EU-registered goods vehicles reached 1,886 billion tonne-kilometres last year, according to newly published Eurostat figures. The tonnage carried rose faster still, up 1.8% to 13.3 billion tonnes, meaning the average load travelled a slightly shorter distance than in 2024 — a sign that growth came from shorter, domestic-style journeys rather than long-haul international runs. ... That pattern is confirmed once the market is broken down by segment. National transport, which already accounted for almost two-thirds of EU road freight activity, grew by 2.2% and now makes up 62.2% of the total. Conventional international transport, where a vehicle’s country of registration matches either the loading or unloading point, managed growth of only 0.3%. ... The segments that fell were the ones with the most cross-border exposure. Cross-trade — a haulier moving goods between two countries neither of which is its country of registration — dropped by 3.7%. Cabotage fell by 3.0%. Together they now account for just 13.4% of total EU road freight activity, having lost ground for a second consecutive year. ... Polish-registered vehicles again recorded the highest transport performance in the EU, completing 381 billion tonne-kilometres in 2025 — 20.2% of the EU total. Germany followed with 277.4 billion tonne-kilometres (14.7%), narrowly ahead of Spain on 272.6 billion (14.5%). France and Italy rounded out the top five, with 172.9 billion and 161.7 billion tonne-kilometres respectively; together, the five largest markets accounted for 67.1% of all EU road freight activity. ... It is worth being precise about what Poland’s ranking measures. Eurostat’s figures record transport by vehicles registered in each country, wherever in the EU that transport takes place. Poland’s leading position therefore reflects the scale of its international haulage sector — including cross-trade and cabotage carried out abroad — rather than domestic freight volumes within Poland itself. Given that cross-trade and cabotage were the two segments that contracted in 2025, Poland’s overall ranking sits somewhat at odds with the pressure facing the specific activities that underpin its international fleet. ... Germany’s role becomes clearer when the data is examined corridor by corridor rather than by national totals. The Germany-Netherlands route was the busiest bilateral flow in the EU, with 86.9 million tonnes transported in 2025, ahead of Germany-Poland (68.4 million tonnes) and Belgium-France (55.9 million tonnes). Germany was the country of loading or unloading in six of the ten largest intra-EU flows — underlining that its centrality to European supply chains lies less in the size of its own registered fleet than in its position as the continent’s principal freight crossroads. ... Taken together, the 2025 figures describe a market that grew, but not evenly. The expansion in national haulage was enough to lift the EU total into positive territory, while the segments that connect national markets to one another — cross-trade and cabotage — continued to lose ground for carriers that rely on them most.

summary_text: CMA CGM withdraws its bid for Rail Logistics Europe, Dutch dockworkers announce a strike, European military personnel inspect a shadow tanker, the Belgian lorry market continues to shrink, Colis Privé and Bleckmann are expanding, ONE sees its profits fall, and Liège Airport is hosting the EU CBEC Forum. ... The French shipping group CMA CGM has withdrawn its bid for a 49 per cent minority stake in the French rail group Rail Logistics Europe (RLE), according to various sources. RLE comprises all the freight operations of the French rail group SNCF, notably Hexafret (formerly Fret SNCF), Captrain France, the combined transport subsidiaries VIIA and Naviland Cargo, Forwardis (freight forwarding/chartering) and Technis (rolling stock maintenance). SNCF intends to partially privatise these activities, and in April 2026 CMA CGM made an offer for a 49 per cent minority stake. SNCF had already engaged several investment banks to oversee the acquisition process. The value of the acquisition is estimated at 800 million euros. In 2025, the freight operations generated turnover of 1.8 billion euros (-1.6 per cent), out of a group turnover of nearly 43 billion euros. It is unclear how matters will proceed from here and whether there are any other candidates. (KH) ... The Dutch trade union FNV Havens has declared Friday 4 September 2026 a national strike day for dockworkers. It informed its members, who work in the ports of Rotterdam, Amsterdam and Zeeland, of this on Monday 3 August. On 4 September, between 11.15 am and 7.00 pm, no ships will be handled. This means that loading, unloading, mooring, towing and cargo inspections may be subject to significant delays. With this nationwide seaport strike, the trade union is demanding that the government immediately withdraw its planned cuts of 6.5 billion euros to social security. Members of FNV Havens decided to go on strike during a general members’ meeting attended by over 700 dockworkers across the Netherlands. (JKV) ... Soldiers from the European mission EURONAVFOR MED IRINI boarded a tanker south of Sicily that is linked to the Russian shadow fleet. The ‘Toa Payoh’ was en route from Cotonou (Benin) to Istanbul, flying the Cameroonian flag. Article 110 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) permits military authorities to verify the nationality of merchant ships if there are serious suspicions that they are sailing under a false flag or without nationality. When the captain did not immediately produce the necessary documentation, Italian marines boarded the vessel by helicopter to carry out an inspection, whilst a Greek naval vessel and a Polish aircraft provided support. After two hours, the operation concluded peacefully without any results being announced. This European mission has been monitoring illegal oil exports from Libya and ensuring general maritime security in the region since 2020. (RJ) ... The market for heavy commercial vehicles in Belgium is in decline. In July 2026, the number of registrations of lorries under 16 tonnes fell by 18.2 per cent month-on-month. This is according to figures from the FPS Mobility and FEBIAC. The 16-tonne and above segment recorded a smaller decline of 1.1 per cent. Cumulatively over the first seven months, both segments remain in the red: -24.4 per cent for the lighter heavy vehicles and -3.7 per cent for the heaviest category. The market for light commercial vehicles also saw a decline in July, with 17.2% fewer registrations than in July 2025. Registration figures in our country run counter to the European trend, where the market for heavy and light commercial vehicles showed a cautious recovery in the first half of 2026. (YDS) ... Colis Privé, a subsidiary of CEVA Logistics, has acquired Paack Ibéria and Paack France. Paack operates in parcel delivery for e-commerce and has its own technological platform and distribution network. With this acquisition, Colis Privé is strengthening its network in France and gaining a foothold in Spain and Portugal, two growth markets for e-commerce. In Spain and Portugal, the company now has 82 branches and more than 5,000 collection points. Around 490 Paack employees will transfer to Colis Privé. Colis Privé also operates in Belgium. (YDS) ... Fashion logistics provider Bleckmann has expanded its partnership with fashion label Karl Lagerfeld. The brand now has a second European fulfilment site at one of Bleckmann’s Spanish distribution centres in Zaragoza, an established logistics hub for the fashion industry. Operations commenced in April 2026 and focus entirely on Karl Lagerfeld’s European outlet channel. This includes warehousing, order picking and packing, as well as B2B deliveries to outlet stores. This complements the brand’s existing European fulfilment centre, which is operated by Bleckmann in Almelo, the Netherlands. Zaragoza is an ideal base for both Southern Europe and pan-European distribution. Bleckmann’s integrated stock management system ensures that stock is expertly coordinated between the two hubs. (KH) ... The Japanese container carrier Ocean Network Express (ONE) closed the first quarter of the 2026 financial year with a net profit of $31 million, compared with $86 million in the same period last year. Revenue did, however, rise slightly from $4 billion to $4.539 billion. According to CEO Till Ole Barrelet, the ongoing disruptions in the Middle East weighed heavily on fuel and operational costs. As the quarter progressed, demand recovered and load factors remained high. Due to this improving market, ONE is raising its profit forecast for the full financial year, although the shipping company says geopolitical uncertainties remain a risk. (SC) ... Liège Airport will host the EU CBEC Forum from 8 to 10 September 2026. The event, organised by Liège Airport in collaboration with the Walloon export agency AWEX, will bring together the international air freight community for high-level discussions, industry insights and networking. High-level industry leaders taking part in the discussions include Jeffrey Van Haeften (Emirates SkyCargo), Mohanned Badri (Saudi Cargo), Peter Scholten (Air One Aviation) and Wolfgang Meier (Silk Way West Airlines). Topics covered at the event include the growing influence of e-commerce on air freight networks, the balance between capacity and demand, changing trade routes, fleet strategies and Liège’s role within European freight operations. (KH)

headline: Transport: EU road freight rose in 2025
summary_text: Transport: EU road freight rose in 2025 ... # Transport: EU road freight rose in 2025 ... ## A total of 13.3 billion tonnes of goods were transported, representing an increase of 1.8 per cent from 2024. The highest volumes were recorded in Poland, Germany, France, Spain, and Italy ... Brussels – The volume of goods transported by road in the European Union has increased. According to Eurostat, the European Union’s statistical office, in 2025, 1,886 billion tonnes-kilometres were moved by road, up 0.9 per cent from the previous year. The total weight of goods transported was 13.3 billion tonnes, marking an increase of 1.8 per cent from 2024. ... The figures show that Poland recorded the highest volume of goods transported by road, at 381.0 billion tonne-kilometres, accounting for 20.2 per cent of the EU total. Germany came second with 277.4 billion (14.7 per cent of the EU total), followed by Spain (272.6 billion; 14.5 per cent), France (172.9 billion; 9.2 per cent), and Italy (161.7 billion; 8.6 per cent). Taken together, the figures for these five countries accounted for 67.1 per cent of the EU total. ... Eurostat points out that in 2025 “The overall distribution of EU road freight transport activity, measured in tonne-kilometres, remained broadly stable.” In particular, most goods were transported domestically (62.2 per cent), while international transport stood at 24.4 per cent. Cross-trade – international road transport between two different countries carried out by a motor vehicle registered in a third country – stood at 10.7 per cent, and cabotage – road transport carried out by a motor vehicle registered in one country travelling within the territory of another country – at 2.7 per cent. Compared with 2024, domestic transport increased by 2.2 per cent, whilst international transport rose by 0.3 per cent. Cross-trade and cabotage fell by 3.7 per cent and 3 per cent, respectively. As regards road freight flows between different EU countries, the largest volume of goods was transported between Germany and the Netherlands, totalling 86.9 million tonnes. In second place was the Germany–Poland route (68.4 million tonnes), followed by Belgium–France (55.9 million tonnes). Germany was the point of origin or destination for six of the top ten EU road freight flows.

headline: What is the state of Germany's HGV charging network? Five key insights - electrive.com
summary_text: If you want to know how many public charging points Germany has, the charging station register maintained by the country’s Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur) is the key reference. As of 1 June 2026, it lists 53,300 publicly accessible DC charging points nationwide. However, if you want to know how many of these can accommodate a 40-tonne truck, you have to dig much deeper. That is exactly what the electrive editorial team has done. Our aim was to assess the current state of Germany’s HGV charging network and track its development over the past few years. ... The earliest reports on HGV charging infrastructure in the electrive archives date back to 2018. At the time, the topic was still largely aspirational. Headlines such as ‘Tesla is already working on an electric truck charging network’ (2018) and ‘ NREL w/ industry test new megawatt charging standard‘ (2021) reflected an industry laying the groundwork for heavy-duty electrification rather than deploying infrastructure at scale. Much of that work has since become reality. This brings us to our first insight: ... One of the first milestones in Germany came in March 2021, when the HoLa(High-Power Charging for Long-Haul Trucking) project brought together industry and research partners to develop a nationwide charging concept for electric trucks. Later that year, the NEFTON consortium, led by the Technical University of Munich, began developing a prototype battery-electric truck with bidirectional megawatt charging capability. At the time, both projects were firmly in the research phase. ... Once Volvo Trucks launched its ... series-produced ... In 2022, Milence emerged as a new player, aiming to build a Europe-wide electric HGV charging network focused initially on Germany. The joint venture is backed by three major electric truck manufacturers, who clearly had no appetite for another round of the chicken-and-egg dilemma and took matters into their own hands. This brings us to the second insight: ... Some operators from the passenger car charging sector also recognised the opportunity and expanded into public truck charging by adapting existing passenger car sites. This, of course, accelerated the process. In 2024, the federal government responded by launching a tender for an initial truck charging network, the counterpart to the Deutschlandnetz, Germany’s nationwide fast-charging programme for passenger cars. The aim was to distribute charging parks nationwide, not just at the most economically attractive locations. ... The rollout was not without obstacles. Germany’s motorway service areas, where most long-distance truck traffic stops, were excluded from the first round of tenders because of an ongoing legal dispute over charging concessions. The litigation had already delayed the rollout of fast chargers for passenger cars and also held back the truck charging programme. This leads us to the third insight: ... We received the answer from Germany’s National Centre for Charging Infrastructure: there are 88 locations with a total of 218 charging stations, which in turn offer 355 charging points. The total installed capacity is around 90,700 kilowatts. ... And: “MCS charging points are now operational for the first time,” the Centre informs us. However, these figures still reflect the status as of the end of April. More recent data is not yet available. Nevertheless, the figures are interesting when compared with those from a year earlier. While the number of charging points has only increased by 85 units, the total installed capacity has surged by 40,540 kW. In other words, Germany is installing an increasing number of ultra-fast HGV charging stations, including MCS charging points with a minimum charging capacity of 700 kW. ... To gain a more up-to-date picture of Germany’s truck charging network, we also turned to the eTrucker app. According to its operators, Germany had 699 HGV-compatible charging locations as of 1 July 2026, grouped into three categories: ... - 154 drive-through locations, where trucks can charge without uncoupling their trailers. This includes dedicated HGV sites as well as passenger car charging parks with sufficient manoeuvring space. The largest operators are Aral Pulse Truck (33 sites), Aral Pulse (17), Milence (10), Shell Recharge (10) and E.ON Drive (7). Seven of these locations already offer at least one MCS charging point: HoLa/Lipperland Süd, Aral sites in Buchholz, Hannover, Schnaittach and Rastow, Energie Südbayern/Dettendorfer near Langenbruck, and ESG Solar near Kassel. ... - 158 locations where uncoupling is recommended but where charging without disconnecting the trailer is possible when space allows. The leading operators are Aral Pulse (34), EnBW (21), Ionity (11) and Autostrom Plus (9). ... - 387 locations where trailers generally need to be uncoupled, although nearby HGV parking is available. EnBW (64), Ionity (52), Shell Recharge (50) and Aral Pulse (49) operate the largest networks in this category. ... At first glance, nearly 700 HGV-compatible charging locations appear to paint a far more optimistic picture than the 88 locations identified by Germany’s National Centre for Charging Infrastructure. The difference, however, stems not only from the more recent data (1 July versus 30 April 2026) but also from methodology. While the National Centre counts publicly funded HGV charging sites, eTrucker classifies charging locations according to their practical usability for trucks. As the company explains, it counts locations rather than plugs because ‘a parking space often has multiple plugs, and if an HGV is charging, another plug may be blocked.’ ... We return to 2024, when a second trend emerged alongside the first public HGV charging sites: semi-public charging. The concept gained traction as logistics pioneers realised their depot chargers were not fully utilised by their own fleets and could also serve trusted haulage partners. The idea spread quickly, fuelled by a spirit of cooperation and supported by manufacturers such as MAN and Daimler Truck. ... The scale of Germany’s semi-public charging network remains difficult to quantify. What is clear, however, is that bureaucratic and digital challenges continue to limit wider adoption. While several initiatives have been launched, they have yet to achieve broad implementation. This leads us to our fourth insight: ... For both public and private or semi-public HGV charging, the federal government has only recently launched funding programmes. The message: both charging scenarios are valid and will ideally interlock closely in the future. For most charging processes, a charging capacity of 400 kW is entirely sufficient. MCS charging operates at an even higher level and is intended to enable battery-electric HGVs to tackle long-haul routes. ... Researchers involved in the HoLa project have also estimated how many public megawatt charging points Germany will need by 2030. Their findings suggest that an initial public fast-charging network with at least 1,000 MCS charging points should be in place by 2030. If battery-electric HGVs achieve rapid uptake in long-haul transport and require charging stops of around 45 minutes, that figure rises to approximately 2,000 MCS charging points by 2030. For comparison, Germany currently has just seven MCS charging points. ... Germany’s HGV charging network is expanding steadily, but the figures also show that its development depends on how charging sites are defined and measured. As battery-electric trucking gathers pace, electrive will continue to track the latest developments. headline: ESTA eyes EU permit reform as new director pushes for harmonised heavy transport rules
summary_text: ESTA eyes EU permit reform as new director pushes for harmonised heavy transport rules ... Miguel Flórez de la Colina. Credit: ESTA Europe. # ESTA eyes EU permit reform as new director pushes for harmonised heavy transport rules #### By Robertha McDonald | Editor 21 July 2026 Europe’s heavy transport industry is closer than ever to achieving meaningful regulatory reform, but success will depend on turning political momentum into practical implementation, according to Miguel Flórez de la Colina, the new Director of the European Association of Abnormal Road Transport and Mobile Cranes (ESTA). ... Speaking shortly after taking over the role on July 1, Flórez said securing approval of the revised EU Weights and Dimensions Directive and the Military Mobility Package represents the industry’s most urgent priority over the next 12 to 18 months. ... Flórez said the proposed revisions have the potential to reshape abnormal transport across Europe by simplifying permitting and creating more consistent operating conditions between member states. ... While discussions with Members of the European Parliament and European Commission officials have been encouraging, he cautioned that regulatory approval is only part of the challenge. ... Even after new legislation is adopted, inconsistent permit processing and administrative practices across individual countries are likely to remain obstacles. ... He noted that obtaining transport permits continues to be slow in several jurisdictions where authorities remain reluctant to modernise bureaucratic procedures. ... ESTA has spent years advocating ... Flórez believes the current legislative process offers the strongest opportunity yet to achieve meaningful harmonisation, although negotiations remain ongoing. ... Without harmonised legislation, regulatory responsibility would increasingly fall back to national and regional governments, creating fragmented requirements that weaken the European single market. ... Flórez also highlighted the rapid growth in the use of Self Propelled Modular Transporters and modular hydraulic trailer systems throughout Europe. ... While these technologies have become essential for transporting increasingly large industrial components, regulatory frameworks have struggled to keep pace. ... To address this, ESTA is developing dedicated training programmes for SPMT operators alongside a series of best practice guides covering modular hydraulic suspended trailers and SPMTs. ... Digital permitting continues to be another area where progress has been slower than many operators expected. ... Flórez said the current legislative proposals include several practical improvements, including one stop permit offices within each country, standardised application forms, multilingual electronic permit systems and wider adoption of Europe wide abnormal load documentation. ... He acknowledged that creating a single digital permitting platform covering the entire European Union remains unrealistic for now. ... However, implementing common digital standards at national level would represent a significant operational improvement for transport companies working across multiple jurisdictions. ... Drawing on more than two decades of experience in heavy lifting and exceptional transport, Flórez said policymakers are increasingly recognising the strategic importance of abnormal transport. ... Although the sector represents only a relatively small part of Europe’s economy, it supports industries ranging from renewable energy and heavy manufacturing to defence infrastructure and major construction projects. ... He said one continuing objective is ensuring governments consider heavy transport requirements when planning new infrastructure rather than addressing them only after projects are complete. ... As Europe continues investing in wind energy, defence capability and industrial development, Flórez believes closer coordination between policymakers and the heavy transport sector will become increasingly important. ... Alongside legislative priorities, ESTA also plans to continue developing the European Crane Operators Licence and the European Trailer Operator Licence, building on initiatives started under former Director Ton Klijn. ... For Flórez, success will ultimately be measured not only by legislation passed in Brussels, but by whether operators experience faster permitting, more consistent regulations and safer working standards across Europe.
