The question of which West African market develops next — and whether Nigeria, with its scale and complexity, can create the conditions for commercial drone delivery — is one of the most significant in the sector's emerging market development. ... The proof of concept for commercial drone delivery in Sub-Saharan Africa was established in Rwanda and Ghana, where Zipline and other operators demonstrated that sustainable, clinically valuable medical logistics operations were achievable. The question of where African drone delivery goes beyond those early markets is one of the most consequential in the sector’s development — because Africa’s healthcare logistics gaps, its geography, and its scale represent a potential market for drone delivery that dwarfs anything that has been achieved to date. ... Nigeria is Sub-Saharan Africa’s most populous country and its largest economy by GDP. Its healthcare logistics challenges are correspondingly large: a population of over 200 million spread across a diverse geography that includes dense coastal urban areas, inland riverine communities, and remote rural regions, served by a healthcare system whose supply chain has chronic reliability and reach limitations. The logistics gap that drone delivery can address is not marginal in Nigeria — it is substantial and consequential for health outcomes at scale. ... The Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority — NCAA — has been developing a regulatory framework for commercial drone operations, including BVLOS applications. The development of this framework has been more complex and slower than in Rwanda or Ghana, reflecting both Nigeria’s regulatory environment and the greater complexity of operating in a densely populated, institutionally complex country compared to the smaller East African markets where drone delivery first proved its concept. ... Several international operators and logistics organisations have conducted engagement with Nigeria around potential drone delivery programmes, attracted by the scale of the opportunity. The translation of that engagement into operational programmes has been limited by regulatory uncertainty, operational complexity, and the challenge of finding sustainable commercial models in a market where healthcare system procurement operates differently from the East African contexts that produced Zipline’s early partnerships. ... Francophone West African countries — including Côte d’Ivoire, Senegal, Mali, and others — have been engaging with drone delivery as a solution to healthcare logistics challenges. One of the structural challenges of African drone delivery expansion is the fragmentation of regulatory frameworks across countries. The African Union and regional bodies including the Economic Community of West African States have engaged with aviation regulatory harmonisation at a general level, but the specific development of harmonised drone regulatory frameworks across African markets remains at an early stage. headline: Kenya’s SHA Reforms Drive Hospital Procurement as WHX Nairobi Brings Healthcare Buyers and Suppliers Together
summary_text: Larmy Majanga August 6, 2026 4 minutes read Kenya’s transition from the National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF) to the Social Health Authority (SHA) is accelerating hospital investment in medical equipment, diagnostics and digital health infrastructure, creating new procurement opportunities ahead of the 10th edition of World Health Expo (WHX) Nairobi, which will take place from 16–18 September 2026 at the Kenyatta International Convention Centre (KICC). ... The shift is part of a broader transformation in East Africa’s healthcare financing landscape, with similar reforms underway in Tanzania, Ethiopia and Uganda. Together, these developments are driving demand for modern healthcare technologies, improved diagnostics, digital hospital systems and more efficient procurement processes. ... As SHA rolls out its Primary Healthcare Fund, Social Health Insurance Fund and Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund, the Ministry of Health reports that more than 31 million Kenyans have registered under the scheme, 11,034 health facilities have been contracted and over KES 147 billion has been paid in claims since October 2024. The expanded coverage and faster reimbursement model are giving healthcare providers greater certainty over patient volumes and revenue, enabling them to plan investments in equipment, digital systems and service delivery. ... Under the new system, primary healthcare providers are reimbursed based on verified patient visits rather than insurance status, while claims processing timelines have been reduced from 90 days to 30 days. These changes are placing greater emphasis on investments in hospital information systems, diagnostics, revenue-cycle management and digital reporting to meet SHA’s data-driven reimbursement requirements. ... Against this backdrop, WHX Nairobi is positioning itself as the region’s leading healthcare procurement and business platform, bringing together hospital executives, procurement leaders, manufacturers, distributors and policymakers to translate healthcare financing reforms into practical purchasing decisions ahead of the next financial cycle. ... 2026 edition is expected to attract more than 5,500 attendees, over 200 exhibitors from more than 30 countries, and feature a 4,500-square-metre exhibition, representing an 81% increase in exhibition space and 22% growth in exhibitors compared to last year. Organisers estimate the 2025 event generated USD 84.19 million in business transactions, demonstrating the exhibition’s growing role in facilitating healthcare investment across East Africa. ... SHA reforms are also influencing procurement priorities through structured reimbursement packages covering inpatient care, maternity services, dialysis, oncology, imaging and diagnostics. Defined reimbursement rates for services such as MRI and CT scans are encouraging hospitals to invest in the equipment and digital systems needed to deliver and accurately claim for these services. ... Across the region, similar reforms continue to strengthen healthcare investment. Ethiopia’s Community-Based Health Insurance programme now covers more than 54 million people, increasing investment in diagnostics, medicines and healthcare quality. Tanzania’s pharmaceutical import market is projected to grow from USD 1.08 billion in 2023 to USD 1.55 billion by 2028, driving demand for medicines, cold-chain infrastructure and digital inventory systems. Uganda continues investing in hospital infrastructure and medical equipment despite constrained public health spending. ... According to World Bank and World Health Organization (WHO) analysis, Africa requires substantially higher private investment in healthcare infrastructure and services to meet growing demand. WHX addresses this need by showcasing innovations across eight product sectors, including medical devices, imaging, laboratory technology, digital health, healthcare infrastructure and hospital services. ... For hospital CEOs, chief operating officers and procurement directors working within the new financing frameworks, investment priorities increasingly include imaging equipment, laboratory systems, electronic medical records (EMRs), pharmacy automation, digital claims management and capacity expansion. ... “Healthcare facilities are under immediate pressure to adapt to new reimbursement structures, expanded benefit packages and digitised claims processing. Across East Africa—from Ethiopia’s CBHI expansion to Tanzania’s pharmaceutical growth and Uganda’s infrastructure investments—we see a shared need for modern medical technologies. WHX provides the commercial platform where healthcare providers can engage directly with global suppliers while gaining a better understanding of the regulatory environment to support long-term investment decisions.” ... Tom Coleman, Portfolio Director – Healthcare at Informa Markets, said healthcare financing reforms are now directly influencing procurement across the region. ... “Healthcare financing reforms across East Africa are no longer theoretical—they are actively reshaping hospital procurement. Kenya’s SHA rollout, Ethiopia’s CBHI expansion, Tanzania’s pharmaceutical sector growth and Uganda’s infrastructure investments are creating urgent procurement needs. WHX brings healthcare leaders together with manufacturers, distributors and technology providers to align investment decisions with these new funding models ahead of the next fiscal year.” ... Coleman added that the WHX portfolio, which includes healthcare exhibitions in Nairobi, Lagos and Johannesburg, continues to connect global healthcare manufacturers with regional distributors and healthcare providers, expanding access to innovative medical technologies across Africa. ... Registration for WHX Nairobi is free for healthcare professionals, procurement leaders and suppliers. As healthcare financing reforms gather pace across East Africa, the September event offers hospitals and industry stakeholders an opportunity to evaluate new technologies, establish partnerships and finalise procurement decisions for the coming financial year.

Chairman of the occasion and Provost of the Federal College of Medical Laboratory Science and Technology, Professor Nkereuwem Etukudoh, said Nigeria was at a defining moment in the evolution of medical laboratory science, urging government at all levels to recognise diagnostics as a strategic national asset rather than a support service. In his words:“There can be no health security without diagnostic security, and there can be no national security without laboratory intelligence. Every solution to our healthcare challenges begins in the laboratory. No laboratory results, no treatment; no data, no policy; no diagnosis, no security.”He described the recent passage by the National Assembly of the bill establishing the Federal University of Medical Laboratory Science and Technology, Jos, as a historic milestone that would position Nigeria as Africa’s leading centre for specialised medical laboratory education, research and innovation.Etukudoh appealed to President Bola Tinubu to promptly assent to the legislation, as the proposed institution would produce highly skilled manpower for disease surveillance, biotechnology, diagnostics, postgraduate training and universal health coverage across the continent.The provost further stated that smart diagnostics required investment in skilled professionals, accredited laboratories, digital health systems, quality assurance and policies that integrate laboratory medicine into national development planning.He warned that pandemics, antimicrobial resistance and emerging pathogens posed threats comparable to conventional security challenges, saying, “The first line of defence against these threats is the medical laboratory scientist. We identify the enemy before it strikes and provide the evidence that drives treatment, policies and national response.” ... The Registrar and Chief Executive Officer of the Medical Laboratory Science Council of Nigeria (MLSCN), Dr. Donald Ofili, in his contribution, proposed a reform agenda aimed at strengthening regulation, transparency, institutional integrity and patient safety within the profession.Ofili argued that the council’s transformation agenda would reposition it as a regulatory body digitally driven, transparent and globally respected institution. Every reform we pursue must ultimately answer one question: Does it improve patient safety? If the answer is yes, we will pursue it with determination.”The MLSCN boss warned tertiary institutions against unethical practices during accreditation exercises, including borrowing laboratory equipment or presenting temporary personnel as permanent staff, saying such actions undermine educational quality and endanger patient safety.He also urged practitioners to embrace ethical conduct, continuous professional development, quality management systems and strict compliance with regulatory standards, while directing that all council payments be made only through approved channels to eliminate fraud.Earlier, the National President of AMLSN, Dr. Casmir Ifeanyi, said modern medical laboratories had become indispensable to disease surveillance, outbreak preparedness, genomic intelligence, blood safety, emergency response and precision medicine.He noted that although Nigeria continues to battle infectious diseases, rising cases of antimicrobial resistance,d non-communicable diseases and the migration of healthcare professionals, strengthening laboratory systems remains one of the most effective strategies for addressing the challenges.“Universal Health Coverage cannot be achieved without Universal Medical Laboratory Coverage. summary_text: ## Africa’s Diagnostic Sovereignty Gap Anafi Mataka, Head of Division at the African Society for Lab Medicine (ASLM) takes on diagnostic sovereignty, AI, and what it really takes to build health systems that last - June 25, 2026 - AI and Innovation, Global insights, Highlight The COVID-19 pandemic forced health systems across the world to confront uncomfortable questions about resilience, self-sufficiency and preparedness. This was especially true for many African countries, where disruptions to global supply chains exposed the extent to which routine healthcare remained dependent on imported tests and laboratory consumables. ... We recently had a thought-provoking conversation with Anafi Mataka, the Head of Division of the African Society of Lab Medicine, an institution that has been at the forefront of shaping diagnostics across Africa for over fifteen years, to discuss the persistent challenges facing African health systems, the progress the organisation has made in advancing diagnostics in Africa, and why he believes the continent is at a pivotal moment when it comes to diagnostic sovereignty. What follows is the full conversation, in his own words. ... In practice, we have identified a theory of change built around four pillars. First, we want to see a sufficient, professionalised, well-governed and well-regulated workforce. You can buy all the machines and equipment you want, you can invest in AI, but without trained people, the system will not be viable. ... Third, we work with national governments to build efficient laboratory networks that are responsive to local needs. And fourth, we work to strengthen the laboratory community itself; its capacity to set its own agenda. We have established the Federation of Laboratory Professionals Associations, a kind of FIFA for lab professionals across the continent, bringing together national associations. We also facilitate the convening of the Laboratory Directors Forum, now covering 44 of Africa’s 55 countries, which creates a space for leaders of national laboratory networks to share practices and drive coordinated progress. ... Alongside all of this, we remain committed to quality assurance. When ASLM started, one of our flagship programmes was Stepwise Laboratory Quality Improvement Process Towards Accreditation (SLIPTA), helping laboratories move stepwise towards accreditation and Strengthening Laboratory Management Toward Accreditation (SLMTA). That work continues. As does our focus on technical innovation, to ensure we stay relevant in a rapidly changing field. ... Beyond the workforce, access to diagnostics is being hampered by a range of structural issues. Many countries still haven’t implemented the Abuja declaration, which calls for 15% of national budgets to be allocated to the health sector. This means laboratories aren’t recognised as critical infrastructure, unless they are national public health laboratories. And you know, since the funding cycle changed, the problem has been amplified even further. ... Geographical barriers and fragmented supply chains are also a challenge. Simple transportation issues and frequent stockouts often affect equity in access within countries. There is also an over-dependence on imported supplies. Basic blood collection tubes are still being imported from Japan, China and abroad. Even basic PPE in some cases. ... And finally, regulatory fragmentation remains a significant barrier. Countries are still independently evaluating and adopting new diagnostics. We need to move toward harmonisation so that innovations can reach communities quickly, at scale. ... African entrepreneurs and tech leaders are already working to bring the infrastructure here. Saudi Arabia and Qatar have made localised large language models freely available as public goods. That is the direction we need to move in, actively shaping AI for our own use. ... Honestly, we have not yet done as much as we should in that space. Our advocacy efforts are active, but we run into a critical obstacle: we lack the economic data that decision-makers require. Governments and finance ministries respond to the cost of inaction. They want to know: what does it cost us not to invest in diagnostics? That data simply does not exist in any comprehensive, Africa-specific form. ... We are currently working on a multi-partner effort to define and quantify the value of diagnostics to build that economic case so it can be placed in front of ministers of finance, ministers of health, and heads of government. We are also working through regional structures and global platforms like the WHO-convened Global Diagnostics Coalition. ... progress is HIV viral load testing across several African countries. Over the past decade, countries have moved from limited access to large-scale testing networks supported by optimised laboratory systems, specimen referral networks, quality management systems, and data-driven decision-making. The lesson is that ... I don’t think we are there. We learned from COVID-19 that when roughly 80 percent of your diagnostics come from outside, you do not have diagnostic sovereignty. And we see this every time we have an issue. When a global crisis hits, countries that produce diagnostic supplies keep them for themselves first, and then supply to the rest of the world. Africa felt this acutely. ... True diagnostic sovereignty requires local manufacturing of diagnostics, not just lip service, but actual production capacity for the supplies and tools the continent needs. There are obviously some efforts that have been put in place there, but this space still needs a lot. We are still importing blood collection tubes and basic PPE from Japan. That needs to change, and it needs sustained political and financial commitment to change it. ... That said, there are positive signals. Countries are now developing Essential Diagnostic Lists — formal, national lists of the tests that every citizen should have access to. For me, this is a sovereignty milestone. When a government publishes an Essential Diagnostic List, it is making a rights-based commitment: these tests are not optional extras, they are what every person in this country is entitled to. The challenge, as always, is implementation. ... ASLM has developed a step-by-step guidance document for countries going through this process, covering everything from forming technical working groups through to submitting the final list to the Ministry of Health for approval. We also provide direct technical assistance to countries that need it. I am glad to say that the large majority of countries that do have a formal Essential Diagnostic List have gone through this process with our support, either directly or alongside other partners. ... If we judge progress solely by the number of accredited laboratories, we might conclude that progress is too slow. However, accreditation was never intended to be a quick intervention. It is a systems-strengthening process that requires leadership, infrastructure, workforce development, quality culture, and sustained investment. ... The more important question is whether accreditation is driving measurable improvements in laboratory quality and patient outcomes. In many countries, laboratories that may never reach immediate accreditation still benefit from implementing quality management principles through programs such as SLIPTA. ... That said, we must be willing to innovate. The future may require more flexible models, greater use of digital tools, stronger peer-learning networks, and risk-based approaches that allow us to improve quality at scale without compromising standards. ... Over the last two decades, African countries have built laboratory networks, expanded molecular testing capacity, strengthened quality systems, developed genomic surveillance platforms, many are now defining essential diagnostic lists and have responded to multiple public health emergencies with increasing sophistication.

headline: TETFund Moves to End Nigeria’s Reliance on Foreign Laboratories For Scientific/Research Analysis - The Pointer
summary_text: TETFund Moves to End Nigeria’s Reliance on Foreign Laboratories For Scientific/Research Analysis - The Pointer ... TETFund Moves ... The Federal Government has intensified efforts to end Nigeria’s dependence on foreign laboratories for scientific testing and research analysis with the establishment of six multi-purpose zonal laboratories under the intervention of the Tertiary Education Trust Fund. This was disclosed on Friday during the presentation of the Advisory Committee’s report on the equipping of the TETFund Multi-Purpose Zonal Laboratories to the Executive Secretary of the Fund, Sonny S. T. Echono, in Abuja. ... Chairman of the Advisory Committee, Chris J. Maiyaki, said the laboratories would serve as strategic national assets capable of transforming Nigeria’s scientific, technological and innovation landscape. ... According to Maiyaki, the committee was inaugurated on February 17, 2026, to advise TETFund on the most efficient and cost-effective scientific equipment required for the six laboratories currently under construction across Nigeria’s geopolitical zones. ... He explained that the committee reviewed several technical documents and conducted verification visits to the host institutions to assess construction progress, equipment requirements and institutional readiness. ... The host institutions include Bayero University Kano, Yakubu Gowon University, University of Lagos, University of Maiduguri, University of Nigeria Nsukka and University of Port Harcourt. ... Maiyaki noted that the construction levels varied across the institutions, with Bayero University Kano recording one of the highest levels of completion, while some others were still at early construction stages. ... He stressed the need for speedy completion of the facilities, warning that deploying sophisticated scientific equipment into unfinished buildings could expose the assets to damage. ... “The laboratories are Nigeria’s answer to a long-standing deficit in scientific infrastructure that has compelled researchers to rely on foreign facilities and limited our ability to translate research findings into innovation and national development,” he said. ... Maiyaki added that the committee developed a consolidated multidisciplinary equipment list covering physical sciences, engineering, life sciences, computing and information technology, as well as high-performance computing infrastructure. ... He further stated that the committee proposed governance and sustainability frameworks aimed at ensuring the laboratories meet international standards and remain functional over time. ... Responding after receiving the report, Echono said the establishment of the laboratories would help Nigeria overcome years of inadequate scientific infrastructure and dependence on foreign facilities for laboratory analysis. According to him, delays experienced during the COVID-19 pandemic exposed the dangers of relying on overseas laboratories for sample testing. ... “The fact that samples had to be taken to the UK, South Africa and even Ghana was a national embarrassment,” Echono said, adding that the new laboratories would reverse the trend once fully operational. ... He disclosed that the projects were being implemented in phases due to funding limitations, noting that four of the laboratories were nearing completion and would soon begin receiving equipment installations. ... Echono explained that TETFund deliberately decided against commissioning empty buildings, opting instead to synchronise equipment procurement and installation with construction progress. ... The TETFund Executive Secretary also said the facilities would operate through a governance framework that encourages partnerships with industries and the private sector to ensure sustainability and accessibility. ... He assured that members of the advisory committee would remain involved during the procurement and installation stages to ensure that supplied equipment meets approved specifications and international standards. ... Stakeholders at the event described the laboratories as a major step toward strengthening Nigeria’s research capacity, boosting innovation and improving the country’s global scientific competitiveness.

headline: ASLTON: Turning research to industry for national growth
summary_text: # Turn research findings into industrial solutions, ASLTON urges members May 12, 2026 12:07 am By Janet Ogundepo The Association of Science Laboratory Technologists of Nigeria has called on its members and relevant stakeholders to turn the several innovations and research outputs generated in universities and research institutions into industrial products and economic power for the nation. The association asserted that it was high time research breakthroughs in the laboratories were moved as materials for industries, stating that the country was sitting on a vast reservoir of scientific knowledge that was yielding little tangible benefit to its economy. The President of ASLTON, Ayotunde Omorilewa, made the call during activities marking the 2026 World Laboratory Day, celebrated globally on April 23 to honour the contributions of laboratory professionals to science, healthcare, public health, and national development. Omorilewa said the central focus of this year’s commemoration was the urgent need to bridge the gap between scientific research and industrial application, describing the current situation as a missed opportunity of significant proportions. ... “The aim of this year’s celebration is how to turn the various research all over our nation, Nigeria, into an industrial breakthrough. Many innovations and research were produced all over Nigeria, including our ivory towers, but little or none are turned into economic power for our nation. It is high time to begin to move en masse our research breakthroughs to materials for our industries,” he said. ... Omorilewa called for urgent collaboration between ASLTON and the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria, arguing that a structured partnership between laboratory professionals and industrial manufacturers was essential to translating scientific findings into commercially viable products. Speaking further, he described the laboratory as “the hub of innovation to all forms of national development and for developing nations like Nigeria, laboratory science is not ... , it is essential. ... TON president further praised the contributions of Science Laboratory Technologists across the country, noting that their work, carried ... the scenes, underpinned healthcare delivery, public health surveillance, environmental monitoring, agricultural development, industrial quality control, and ... research nationwide. ... “From tertiary institutions to hospitals, from research institutes to industrial laboratories, Science Laboratory Technologists are indispensable to Nigeria’s progress,” he said. He, however, acknowledged that the profession continued to operate under significant constraints, citing inadequate laboratory infrastructure, limited funding for research and laboratory services, shortages of modern equipment and reagents, and workforce development gaps as pressing challenges that required attention. Omorilewa stressed the need for the Federal Government to put in place enabling policies and professional recognition for laboratory scientists across all sectors. Omorilewa further called on the government to step up the fight against quackery in the profession and specifically urged the Head of Service to remove clauses in the civil service rules and employment criteria that he said actively promoted the employment of unqualified individuals over core laboratory professionals. He admonished his colleagues to pursue continuous professional training, certification, and recertification programmes, and to embrace emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, as tools to aid laboratory productivity.

Prime Minister Russell Mmiso Dlamini, who is currently in the Republic of China (Taiwan), held strategic trade talks with representatives of the Taiwan Packaging Association in Taipei yesterday. ... Australia uses more than 1.3 million tonnes of plastic packaging every year, yet only 19 per cent is collected for recycling. More than one million tonnes is landfilled or littered annually. ... Toumbourou said the reason is not a lack of technology. Around the country, an estimated 320,000 tonnes of Australian plastic reprocessing capacity is standing ready, much of it sitting idle. She said the Australian Government’s failure to deliver promised packaging reform is putting recyclers in commercial peril with some plants facing closure. ... “What makes the delay so hard to justify is the cumulative cost of doing nothing, which could exceed $32 billion by 2050, while plastic waste in Australia rises to almost five million tonnes a year,” Toumbourou said. ... “All the while, sophisticated recycling facilities are operating below capacity. Recyclers invested in the infrastructure, technology and skills needed to remanufacture plastic packaging in Australia on the strength of government commitments to reform. They have now been left in dire straits by repeated delay.” ... In 2023, Australia’s environment ministers committed to national packaging reform by 2025, including mandatory standards for packaging design, recyclability and recycled content. The Australian Government has still not delivered those reforms. ... Toumbourou said that without national requirements and incentives to use Australian recycled content, local recyclers are being undercut by cheaper imported plastic. National utilisation of plastic recycling infrastructure is about 50 per cent and could fall to 30 per cent by 2030 without action. ... “The Australian Government helped fund recycling plants and prohibited the export of unprocessed plastic waste but failed to create the regulatory and market settings needed for that material to be remade into new products,” she said. ... “That failure now threatens the very facilities the government helped fund. Facilities cannot survive indefinitely at half capacity. Once plants close, Australia loses the equipment, workforce, technical expertise and sovereign capability needed to recycle its own plastic.” ... She said Europe provides a warning. About one million tonnes of European plastic recycling capacity was lost between 2023 and 2025 as recyclers were squeezed by weak demand, high operating costs and cheap imports. Australia is now following the same path. ... Modelling shows reform could cut wasted plastic by 370,000 tonnes a year, reduce emissions by 700,000 tonnes annually, generate $2.5 billion in economic activity, support almost 20,000 Australian jobs and attract a further $220 million in private investment. Continued inaction, by contrast, means plant closures, lost jobs, more plastic waste and deeper dependence on imported virgin plastic. ... “The cost of reform is negligible. The cost of Australian Government delay is staggering,” Toumbourou said. “The government must commit to a firm timeline to introduce mandatory national packaging laws that hold producers responsible for the packaging they place on the market and drive demand for Australian recycled content. ... “Plastic Free July is ending with more plastic going to waste and Australian recycling capacity at risk of shrinking. Australians have done their part. Industry has invested. The Australian Government must now commit to firm timeframes this year and get on with the job.” ... ### ACOR proposes new Trigger Framework for product stewardship schemes ... ### ACOR, APCO build the case for Australian recycling plastics

headline: Amendments made to the Plastic Reduction and Circular Economy Act 2021 - ProPack
summary_text: Amendments made to the Plastic Reduction and Circular Economy Act 2021 - ProPack ... Amendments made to the Plastic Reduction and ... 202 ... 22 July, ... 026 ... APCO's Peter Brisbane gives us a review of the new bill ... The Environmental Legislation Amendment (Plastic Reduction and Container Recycling) Bill 2026 was recently tabled in NSW Parliament. ... Australian Packaging Covenant Organisation (APCO) head of government partnerships Peter Brisbane reviewed the bill and stated, “The purpose of the bill is to amend a bunch of environmental legislation, mostly of minor interest – for example being able to share information relating to contaminated sites with commonwealth and interstate regulators, and other compliance provisions. ... “There are three things that are significant to packaging and give effect to parts of the NSW Plastics Plan 2.0.” Brisbane said these are: ... - Under the Plastics Reduction and Circular Economy Act 2021: there are additional provisions concerning design standards and new provisions supporting reusable cups. - Under the Waste Avoidance and Resource Recovery Act 2001: there are changes to CDS, particularly tethered caps. ... amendments to the ... 2021 ... - The Plastics Plan 2.0 committed to a range of design and labelling requirements for single use plastic items including: ... - - Takeaway food and beverage packaging to be recyclable by 2028. ... - Labelling for proper disposal on single use plastic cups, food containers and plastic bags by 2028. - Some other items to be recyclable and labelled for for proper disposal by 2030. ... - The bill adds a couple of paragraphs to the existing provisions of the Plastic Reduction and Circular Economy Act 2021 concerning: ... - - The EPA having authority to make decisions concerning design standards in relation to labelling or recyclability. ... - A design standard in relation to recyclability to incorporate or adopt a publication as in force for the time being or from time to time. ... - A beneficial ... of the new ... could be for design ... in NSW to refer directly to publications such as national design standards, Sustainable Packaging Guidelines or ARL documentation. Reusable cups: - The Plastics Plan 2.0 committed to scaling up reuse models to replace single-use plastics, particularly cups. - The bill effectively establishes a scheme to support reusable cups in takeaway businesses. ... - The scheme does not ban single-use cups; instead, it requires that reuse options be provided. Businesses selling takeaway beverages must: - - Use a reusable cup if one is provided by the customer, and must not charge the customer for using that cup with the commencement date of this requirement set as 2028. ... - Make a reuse scheme reusable cup available to the customer, and must not charge a fee for the reuse scheme reusable cup with the commencement date of this requirement set at 2030. ... - A reuse scheme is defined as ... reusable cups. ... - There’s a lot of detail on definitions, compliance, record keeping and information gathering, and a provision prohibiting false information about reuse schemes. ... - Commentary: NSW will be the first jurisdiction to establish a requirement for reusable cups. In addition, he mentioned amendments to the Waste Avoidance and Resource Recovery Act 2001 include: Circular economy and waste hierarchy ... Beverage containers: ... - The Plastics Plan 2.0 commits to requiring tethered caps for containers 1.25 litres and below, from 2030. - The bill adds principles of a circular economy to the objects of the part of the Act that establishes the CDS, which will enable it to address container design. - The bill establishes that certain opening mechanisms can be banned. - This will enable tethered caps to be effectively mandated, by banning non-tethered caps. ... - There are a couple of other amendments to the CDS including a new requirement for containers to have a prescribed barcode and a maximum term for scheme coordinator and network operator agreements of 20 years, including initial agreements and extension. ... - Commentary: NSW will be the first jurisdiction to require tethered caps.

headline: Island nations call for packaging redesign to curb ocean plastic
summary_text: # Island nations call for packaging redesign to curb ocean plastic ... - Island nations face mounting plastic pollution amid limited recycling infrastructure and dependence on imported packaging. - Experts advocate reuse systems, DRS, and EPR. - Industry and governments are urged to eliminate problematic packaging before it reaches island markets. ... Despite efforts in the packaging industry to address rising levels of plastic packaging pollution with innovations in fiber-based, reusable, and recycled-content solutions, ocean-bound plastic remains a prevalent issue, especially for island nations. ... Ocean plastic pollution disproportionately affects island nations, which lack the infrastructure and investment to process large amounts of packaging waste. In one modeled scenario of no improvement to global waste management, the researchers estimate that by 2060, there will be 2.8 times more ocean plastic than in 2018. ... One initiative is the Australian Government-funded Pacific Ocean Litter Project (POLP), which aims to reduce marine plastic litter in Pacific island countries. ... Halatoa Fua, director for the National Environment Service for the Cook Islands, a POLP participating country, tells us that industry and governments must work together to reduce unnecessary packaging and ensure that it can be reused, recovered, exported, or managed in island markets. ... “For island economies, the challenge is not only waste management, but also product design, import dependency, shipping costs, limited land availability, and the absence of large-scale recycling infrastructure.” ... Meanwhile, conservation expert and former president of the Samoa Conservation Society, James Atherton, tells us that packagers need to switch to reusable packaging such as glass for beverages and promote biodegradable solutions. ... Last year, Coca-Cola switched from reusable glass bottles to plastic bottles in Samoa, while a recent study found that F&B plastic packaging is one of the most common sources of litter on the world’s coastlines. ... There is increasing scrutiny on major F&B corporations to take responsibility for the packaging pollution they might produce by reducing production. A study found that, from 2000 to 2023, Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, and Nestlé produced around 138 million metric tons of plastic, of which 8% to 11% was recycled. ... Atherton and Fua each note that reducing plastic production, especially of single-use items, is key to reducing the pressure of plastic pollution on island communities. ... Dr. Dana Miller, Oceana’s senior director of Strategic Initiatives, also tells us that a lot of F&B packaging is not needed or could be replaced with reusable packaging. ... and environmental groups’ push for plastic reduction is, at times, at odds with the packaging industry’s ... to protect products. This is especially prevalent for F&B ... . Switching to non- ... materials can result in performance trade-offs that led to increased food waste, which is also a ... environmental concern. ... For island nations, Fua explains that “the most practical circular packaging models are those that are simple, enforceable, and suited to small and dispersed markets.” ... “Deposit return systems (DRS) for beverage containers, refill and reuse models for water and household products, community-based recovery schemes, and regional aggregation of recyclable materials have shown strong potential,” he adds. ... F&B corporations and packaging producers are also pursuing lightweighting and recyclability as another means to reduce plastic. Packaging Insights recently spoke to Paritosh Ladhani, managing director at SLMG Beverages, a Coca-Cola distributor, who told us that the industry is moving toward lightweight PET, recyclable materials, and packaging formats designed for a circular economy. ... Reusable packaging options are fast becoming one example of packaging that can effectively reduce plastic pollution and support circular systems. ... However, reuse system companies Borealis, Tomra, and Eco-Products previously explained to us that scaling reuse systems relies on close value-chain collaboration. ... “Reusable containers go through repeated industrial dishwashing, handling, and transport, and are subject to mechanical stress throughout,” Peter Voortmans, VP for Marketing Consumer Products at Borealis told Packaging Insights. “So they need to be designed with those conditions in mind.” ... Miller at Oceana notes that “refillable glass bottling systems have operated all over the world for decades. Despite being replaced with single-use plastic bottles and cans in many places, they still exist in some countries and work at scale.” ... She also adds that there is too much focus on plastic recycling and recycled content as a solution to plastic pollution. ... “Plastic recycling is ... as plastic is ... an infinitely recyclable material, and there are many types of plastic, which complicates and contaminates the plastic recycling process,” she attests. ... Fua argues that while reuse systems have potential, they work best when backed by clear import controls, EPR schemes, reliable collection systems, and financing for transport and export. ... “Tools such as EPR, DRS, reuse targets, and packaging import rules must be adapted to the realities of island economies,” he underscores. ... In recent years, legislation has attempted to install ocean plastic pollution prevention policies. Last year, the third UN Ocean Conference concluded with a joint call to expand marine protection and curb ocean pollution. The UN Global Plastics Treaty, despite failing to pass, includes articles that aim to mitigate ocean plastic pollution. ... “For the Cook Islands, the UN Global Plastics Treaty must recognize the special circumstances of Small Island Developing States. Islands are on the frontline of plastic pollution but often have the least capacity to manage the products and packaging imported into their economies,” says Fua. ... Miller also places emphasis on governments and regulators to support reusable packaging and introduce EPR’s that make it “less appealing to continue selling products in single-use plastic packaging.” ... Miller points out that global organizations, including those in the packaging sector, can increase awareness among the public about reusable packaging and “shift away from our global reliance on single-use plastic.” ... Recent industry efforts have included the TUI Care Foundation’s expansion of its recycling project in Curaçao. Senior manager for Program Development at the TUI Care Foundation, Ivory Hackett-Evans, said that packaging producers can support more circular packaging systems by designing packaging that is manageable in an island context. ... Last year, Chomps, a US-based snack brand, announced a collaboration with 4ocean, a global clean-up organization, to help reduce plastic pollution in the ocean. ... However, Atherton argues that “much stronger” action is needed to enforce circular policies from packaging producers and governments alike. ... For Fua, the path forward is clear: “The most effective solution is to stop problematic plastic packaging before it becomes waste, before it reaches our islands, and before it enters our ocean.”

headline: RMIT and EFWA launches sustainable food packaging centre - Food & Beverage Industry News
summary_text: RMIT and EFWA launches sustainable food packaging centre - Food & Beverage Industry News ... RMIT and EFWA launches sustainable food packaging centre ... The Food and Beverage Small and Medium Enterprise Packaging and Machinery Solution Centre has been launched by RMIT and End Food Waste Australia CRC (EFW CRC) to support SMEs transitioning to reusable, recyclable and compostable packaging and processing solutions. ... Led by RMIT and the EFW CRC, the The Food and Beverage Small and Medium Enterprise Packaging and Machinery Solution Centre will provide independent, research based support to SMEs transitioning to reusable, recyclable and compostable packaging and processing solutions while maintaining product quality and shelf life. ... The centre is a collaboration between RMIT University, End Food Waste Australia, the Australasian Institute of Packaging (AIP), the Australian Packaging and Processing Machinery Association (APPMA) and Tetra Pak. ... It will deliver co-funded applied research and technical expertise to help SMEs assess packaging innovations and processing changes aligned with Australia’s circular economy and sustainable packaging goals. ... Executive director at the Australasian Institute of Packaging, Nerida Kelton, said the centre would help SMEs better understand changing packaging requirements. ... “The shifting landscape of packaging regulations, both domestically and globally, are changing the way companies need to design. Key areas of change include becoming recycle ready, moving to mono materials, building in recycled content and looking at ways to reduce the amount of packaging wherever possible,” Kelton said. ... “Important changes include designing for accessibility and inclusivity, looking at how packaging can potentially minimise food loss and waste across a value chain and looking at viable alternatives that can reduce the carbon footprint of the packaging. The new centre will allow SME’s to have access to technical consultants from the AIP who can help their packaging journey.” Kelton said ... Chief executive officer at the Australian Packaging and Processing Machinery Association, Michael Moran, said the initiative would connect research with practical manufacturing solutions. ... provides an important ... Director of corporate affairs at Tetra Pak, Flavia Vaz, said reducing food waste remained a focus for the company’s packaging and processing work. ... “Our solutions are designed to protect food, extend shelf life and reduce environmental impact across the value chain. From aseptic processing and packaging that protect perishable food, to creating value from by-products, we invest in integrated technologies that reduce waste and improve efficiency. ... Alongside co funded research, the centre will connect SMEs with technical experts from industry and academia. Research delivery will be supported by EFW CRC partner institutions including RMIT University, Queensland University of Technology (QUT), The University of Queensland (UQ) and the South Australian Research and Development Institute (SARDI), among others. ... SMEs can participate through a rolling expression of interest process available via the End Food Waste Australia website. Eligible Australian based SMEs with a valid ABN will be invited to apply and, if successful, contribute matched cash funding on a dollar for dollar basis for approved projects.

headline: Ravenwood selects Wedderburn to expand linerless labelling in Australia

Ravenwood Packaging said Wedderburn Australia has been added to its international network as an authorised distributor of machinery and a print partner. ... It is also set to install a Ravenwood Com500 linerless coating system, allowing linerless labels to be manufactured within Australia. ... Ravenwood said the arrangement means Wedderburn will be able to supply a full linerless labelling offering with local expertise. ... Ravenwood Packaging managing director Paul Beamish said: “Australia represents an important growth market for linerless technology, and we’re excited to be partnering with Wedderburn to expand the availability of our solutions across the region. ... “By combining Ravenwood’s linerless machinery and coating technology with Wedderburn’s established market presence and technical expertise, we’re creating a strong platform to support customers looking to improve efficiency, reduce waste and adopt more sustainable labelling practices.” ... Established in 1896, Wedderburn is a family-owned business that operates in Australia and New Zealand across labels, labelling systems, weighing equipment, packaging machinery and food technology. ... The company has also taken part in initiatives aimed at cutting packaging waste and improving recyclability, including the use of FSC-certified materials, involvement in circular economy schemes such as RafCycle, and collaboration with industry bodies focused on packaging sustainability and compostable materials. ... Wedderburn executive chairman Philip Wedderburn said: “This partnership represents an exciting step forward in our commitment to delivering innovative and sustainable labelling solutions to the Australian market. ... “Ravenwood has established itself as a global leader in linerless technology and we are proud to become both an approved distributor of its machinery and printer partner for linerless labels. Together, we look forward to helping Australian businesses access proven linerless solutions that support greater efficiency, reduced waste and improved sustainability outcomes.”

headline: Paper industry struggles with declining production - packaging journal
summary_text: Paper industry struggles with declining production - packaging journal ... In the first half of 2026, the German paper industry is facing declining production and sales. Association President Gallenkamp is urgently calling for economic policy reforms. ... The economic situation of the German paper and pulp industry did not improve in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period last year. Despite hopes for an economic recovery, the turnaround has failed to materialize. Production and turnover in the German paper and pulp industry continue to decline, according to the current half-year balance sheet from the German Paper Industry Association (Die Papierindustrie). ... A key factor inhibiting the industry's recovery is the poor business environment in Germany. High energy prices, strict environmental regulations and comparatively high labour costs make it difficult for companies to compete internationally. Association President Hans-Christoph Gallenkamp emphasises the urgency of economic policy reforms. „Economic policy reforms must now pick up speed. There must not be another year of stagnation.“ ... As a basic materials industry, the sector remains closely tied to macroeconomic demand trends and international value chains. Production and turnover declined further: the production volume fell to 9.4 million tonnes (-1.4 per cent) and turnover to 6.9 billion euros (-7.1 per cent). ... Packaging papers remained the largest category by volume at 6.4 million tonnes (+/-0 percent), accounting for more than 67 percent of total production. Despite lower volumes (722,000 tonnes, -0.8 percent), technical and speciality papers held their ground as an important pillar for sales and revenue. Graphic papers achieved the second-largest production share at 18 percent, but again fell significantly by 6.9 percent to 1.7 million tonnes. Tissue papers were also 2.0 percent below the previous year at 658,000 tonnes. ... The association is calling for permanently more competitive energy costs, faster planning and approval procedures, and a comprehensive reduction in bureaucratic burdens and reporting obligations. The social security systems must also be stabilised and more strongly geared towards employment and performance incentives. These are the prerequisites for future investments in state-of-the-art production facilities in order to secure value creation and employment at the Germany location in the long term. „Industrial competitiveness must once again become the guiding principle of political action. Companies only invest if the locational conditions are right,“ said Gallenkamp. ... Instead of facilitating investments in climate-neutral production, additional costs and bureaucratic requirements are increasingly burdening companies. This applies in particular to the planned ETS reform. The European Commission's proposal to oblige companies to make potentially uneconomic investments up to the amount of free allocation has met with sharp criticism from industry. „Companies are committed to the transformation. However, central prerequisites are often lacking – from climate-neutral energy sources to sufficient grid capacities and market-ready technologies. Anyone who creates ever new regulations under these conditions jeopardises investments and accelerates the deindustrialisation of the business location,“ emphasises Gallenkamp.

headline: Crude oil concerns drive up costs, but supply holds
summary_text: Crude oil concerns drive up costs, but supply holds ... ALAN GELDER Crude oil is the foundation for all petrochemical and feedstock prices ... SANTIAGO CASTRO The primary impact in the PX/PTA sector was pricing-related rather than outright shortages ... MOHAMED CHILMERAN North American MEG production has been the natural alternative for Asian buyers ... While the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has increased paraxylene (PX), purified terephthalic acid (PTA) and mono ethylene glycol (MEG) prices, outright supply shortages have been limited, with high crude oil prices being the dominant cost driver across the petrochemicals value chain, according to global research and consultancy group Wood Mackenzie. ... Around 20% of Europe’s PX supply comes from the Middle East, a share that has grown with the addition of a new PTA asset in Türkiye. Middle Eastern supply accounts for only 5% to 10% of the US’s PX, with a similar share for the rest of the world, says Wood Mackenzie senior research analyst Santiago Castro. ... Consequently, the primary impact was pricing-related rather than outright shortages, owing to feedstock price increases lifting costs across the board. ... He notes that a genuine uncertainty is a PX asset in Kuwait that has not produced since the start of March, following State-owned hydrocarbon company Kuwait Petroleum Corporation’s force majeure declaration. It is confirmed that the unit was shut down owing to Hormuz-related export and feedstock disruptions rather than physical damage, however, the surrounding Shuaiba industrial zone has since been struck. Given the lack of confirmed damage to the unit itself, a restart is possible once the conflict ends. ... Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia continued shipping from its western Red Sea coast throughout the conflict, and product continued flowing into Europe which built up inventories rather than draining them. ... Castro notes that European buyers initially moved quickly to secure supply from domestic producers, pushing prices up sharply in March and April, but almost immediately reverted to a wait-and-see posture as imports continued. ... In contrast, Asia experienced more acute impacts as the Middle East supplies a significant share of the naphtha that feeds Asian PX, PTA and polyester chains, with many Asian countries struggling to source naphtha as a result. ... Castro says Asia experienced significant capacity-related impacts as some countries prioritised fuel production over petrochemicals, constraining feedstock availability and prompting producers to bring forward planned maintenance or reduce production. ... While a significant volume of Asian capacity has been offline, some units have already begun returning to production, says Castro. ... Similarly, with regard to MEG, the most acute impacts have been in Asia, particularly China, India and Southeast Asia, given Saudi Arabia and Kuwait’s roles as major producers, says Wood Mackenzie market analyst Mohamed Chilmeran. ... He explains that Saudi Arabia’s larger production base sits on its eastern coast, which has been impacted by the disruption, with only partial coverage from its Red Sea facilities. Meanwhile Kuwait’s position meant that Asia absorbed the sharpest supply shortfall, which was compounded by the naphtha feedstock shortage. ... North American production has been the “natural alternative” for Asian buyers, as costs are broadly comparable to Middle Eastern supply, while in Europe, Saudi Arabia’s reduced availability resulted in shortfalls in the Mediterranean region. ... Two significant drivers of MEG production shutdowns were a dearth of feedstock in Asia and trade flow disruption from the Strait blockage, says Chilmeran, who adds that since the MEG markets were oversupplied, the current disruption is primarily trade flow rebalancing rather than genuine capacity shortage. ... Chilmeran adds that the primary challenge was timing, because when the conflict began, North American operating rates were still depressed, driving a sharp price spike and a rush to secure product. ... Industry Dynamics Crude oil is the foundation for all petrochemical and feedstock prices, making the chemicals industry largely a price-taker from the broader energy market, explains Wood Mackenzie Macro Oils senior VP Alan Gelder. ... On the PX side, feedstock costs are closely tied to gasoline markets, particularly in the US and Europe. Therefore, even if the Strait reopens and crude prices soften, PX feedstock prices in Europe and the US are likely to remain elevated until September, when seasonal gasoline demand falls and specifications change, Castro says. ... Chilmeran adds that ethylene oxide (EO) prices jumped nearly 15% immediately after the crisis began, reflecting their direct link to ethylene, naphtha or ethane and ultimately oil prices. However, EO assets typically have flexibility to shift output between the glycols unit and the purified EO unit depending on where demand and margins are strongest. ... “Feedstock cost movements and product availability constraints exerted notable pressure on prices across glycols and EO derivatives,” Chilmeran says. ... Polyethylene terephthalate plastic, which depends on PTA and MEG, has faced simultaneous pressure on both inputs. Polyester producers have experienced the largest impact, with margins squeezed significantly, compounded by weaker polyester demand in Europe and the US independent of the closure of the trade or the increase in prices. ... “After a disappointing 2025, we had anticipated a stronger recovery this summer. Instead we’re navigating both subdued demand and elevated input costs simultaneously,” says Castro. ... A prolonged closure through year-end, which is not Wood Mackenzie’s base case, would have consequences well beyond petrochemicals. Oil prices could more than double current levels, tipping the global economy into stagflation, Gelder explains. ... In that scenario, the chemicals industry would face simultaneously high input costs and collapsing demand, which would be felt across the entire value chain.

headline: Ethylene spreads keep falling, clouding petrochemical sector's second-half outlook - The Herald Business
summary_text: Ethylene spreads keep falling, clouding petrochemical sector's second-half outlook - The Herald Business ... spreads keep falling, clouding ... sector's second-half outlook ... Renewed Middle East conflict risks are deepening uncertainty for South Korea's petrochemical industry. The ethylene spread — the difference between ethylene and naphtha prices, and a key profitability gauge for petrochemical companies — has been falling steadily, raising concerns about deteriorating earnings in the second half. ... According to raw materials price data from the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, the ethylene spread averaged about $315 per ton in April and $135.3 per ton in June, before falling to $100 per ton on Thursday — roughly one-third of its April level in just three months. The industry generally regards $250 to $300 per ton as the breakeven threshold, meaning the current spread falls well short of that mark. ... Naphtha prices surged earlier this year on supply disruption fears following armed conflict between the United States and Iran in the first quarter. Monthly average prices spiked to $1,018.64 per ton in March and $1,063.14 in April, but quickly stabilized after a ceasefire agreement eased Middle East supply chain anxiety, falling to $708.41 in June. In July (July 1–28), however, prices rebounded to $798.1 per ton. ... Monthly average ethylene prices also climbed sharply, nearly doubling from $663.75 per ton in February to $1,216.25 in March before surging further to $1,378 in April. Prices then retreated to $1,097.5 in May and $843.75 in June, edging back up to $852.5 in July (July 1–24). The pattern points to a troubling divergence: renewed Middle East tensions pushed raw material costs higher in July while product prices remained weak, raising the prospect of negative margins. ... Earlier this year, the petrochemical industry turned profitable in the first quarter as product prices rose amid the escalating Middle East war. The improvement came as surging international oil prices — driven by the conflict around the Strait of Hormuz in March — allowed companies to sell products made from cheaper, previously stockpiled raw materials at elevated prices, widening margins. ... That inventory lagging effect — where cheaper raw materials purchased earlier are reflected in costs only after a delay — is believed to have continued into the second quarter. Naphtha prices in April and May, which feed into second-quarter earnings, remained elevated, while the softening in raw material costs that followed the ceasefire only began to appear in June, limiting its impact on second-quarter results. ... The operating environment for the second half looks increasingly difficult. The industry faces a dilemma in which either direction of Middle East geopolitical risk carries a cost. If tensions persist at current levels, high oil prices will keep naphtha costs elevated while weak downstream demand prevents ethylene prices from recovering — leaving little or no profit margin on sales. ... Conversely, even a dramatic resolution to the conflict that sends oil and naphtha prices sharply lower would offer little relief. Companies would then face a reverse lagging effect — having to sell products made from expensive raw materials at lower prevailing prices — triggering a sharp near-term earnings decline. ... The industry consensus is that earnings improvements driven by external variables have their limits unless genuine downstream demand recovery accompanies any easing of the global economic slowdown. Against this backdrop, domestic petrochemical companies are expected to accelerate structural restructuring in the second half. The government recently approved a second petrochemical restructuring project in Yeosu, following the first in Daesan. In Ulsan, however, restructuring discussions remain complicated by S-Oil's 9 trillion won ($6.25 billion) Shaheen Project, scheduled for completion in November.

headline: The 50:50 restructuring of South Korea's two petrochemical giants is blocked, with the FTC citing monopoly risks. - ChemNet
summary_text: The 50:50 restructuring of South Korea's two petrochemical giants is blocked, with the FTC citing monopoly risks. - ChemNet ... # The 50:50 restructuring of South Korea's two petrochemical giants is blocked, with the FTC citing monopoly risks. 2026-07-30 09:10:41 Source:ChemNet 中文 On July 29, the Korea Fair Trade Commission (KFTC, referred to as FTC) publicly updated the review progress of the large-scale restructuring project between Lotte Chemical and HD Hyundai Daesan Petrochemical. This project is a benchmark for the structural adjustment of South Korea's petrochemical industry. Currently, the antitrust investigation is continuing to advance, and regulators have explicitly stated that they maintain a high level of concern regarding market monopoly risks in the domestic LDPE and EVA sectors. ... According to the restructuring plan, Lotte Chemical and HD Hyundai Oilbank will jointly establish an integrated petrochemical complex with a 50-50 equity stake. The implementation path involves Lotte Chemical spinning off assets from its Daesan plant and merging them into HD Hyundai Chemical. The two parties will integrate two naphtha cracking centers (NCC) within the Daesan Industrial Complex, while simultaneously coordinating the integrated operation of their full series of LDPE and EVA polyolefin production capacities. By achieving cost reductions through facility synergy and optimizing the allocation of raw materials and finished product sales, they aim to cope with the long-term downturn in the global petrochemical industry. ... Since accepting the merger filing in November 2025, the South Korean FTC has completed market research on over 20 petrochemical products, with core controversies focusing on two major categories: Low-Density Polyethylene (LDPE) and Ethylene-Vinyl Acetate Copolymer (EVA). Regulatory authorities pointed out that the merger of the two enterprises will occupy an extremely high share of the domestic market, posing risks of dual competitive harm: first, the synergistic effect, where a reduction in the number of competitors makes it easier for enterprises to manipulate product prices and supply volumes in unison; second, unilateral market power, where if the complex unilaterally raises prices, other manufacturers in the industry will find it difficult to quickly supplement alternative sources, thereby squeezing the profit margins of downstream enterprises in packaging, photovoltaic encapsulant films, footwear materials, and other terminal sectors. ... To eliminate antitrust concerns, Lotte and Hyundai Petrochemical have submitted revised remedial plans to regulators over multiple rounds, including restrictive clauses such as supply obligations, pricing constraints, and capacity release commitments. The FTC Secretariat has issued a review report and given a preliminary opinion for conditional approval; however, a full commission meeting has not yet been held to finalize the resolution. On July 29, the regulator disclosed that the review is still deepening and the final approval result has not yet been issued. ... Industry analysts believe that if this restructuring is successfully implemented, the Daesan petrochemical base in South Korea will form a highly competitive integrated cracking-polyolefin production cluster in East Asia, significantly boosting South Korea's export competitiveness in EVA photovoltaic materials. However, if the antitrust constraint clauses are stringent, it may limit the joint venture's capacity allocation and pricing flexibility for external sales, thereby prolonging the project implementation cycle. Currently, the global supply pattern for EVA and LDPE remains stable, and the progress of this review will directly impact the medium-to-long-term supply expectations for polyolefins in Northeast Asia.

Still, the oil correction did little to reverse sellers’ firmer stance.Rather than triggering renewed price erosion, the decline in crude merely reinforced buyers’ resistance to further increases. The broader market tone remained noticeably firmer than in previous months, although any sustained upward trend will still depend on a post-holiday recovery in demand.After several months of continuous price erosion, Europe’s PP and PVC markets appear to have reached a temporary floor. The recent recovery in crude oil and feedstock costs has not been sufficient to reverse the prevailing weak-demand environment, but it has brought the downtrend that began in May to a halt. As a result, expectations for August are centered on largely stable prices, although suppliers are expected to test modest hike requests depending on the August monomer settlements and any further shifts in the geopolitical and energy landscape. Southeast Asia: Buyer hesitation rises, sellers remain resilientThe sharp swings in crude oil had a greater impact on buyer behavior than on pricing strategies across Southeast Asia’s PP and PE markets. Buyers became increasingly reluctant to commit to fresh purchases as energy prices fluctuated rapidly, preferring to cover only immediate needs. Sellers, however, largely maintained firm offers, supported by replacement costs and expectations that upstream markets could remain volatile.As a result, the oil correction slowed trading activity rather than reversing the market’s underlying direction. The gap between buyers and sellers widened, but bullish pricing sentiment remained largely intact.China: Cost-driven rally loses momentum China’s polymer markets emerged as the clearest exception to the broader global trend. After staging a two-week rally on the back of stronger crude oil, feedstock prices and firmer Dalian futures, the market quickly lost momentum as oil prices turned sharply volatile. The abrupt reversal exposed the rally’s heavy reliance on upstream cost support rather than improving fundamentals.Falling crude prices weighed on Dalian futures, which in turn pressured domestic spot PE, PP and PVC markets. Across the PE market, HDPE and LLDPE film prices moved lower, while LDPE film largely held its ground. Import PP and PE offers initially remained firm before gradually softening by mid-week in line with weaker domestic sentiment.Weak seasonal demand continued to discourage buying, while unpredictable movements in crude oil and futures markets made both buyers and sellers increasingly cautious.Türkiye: Tight polyolefin supply outweighs crude correction Türkiye’s polymer markets remained largely unaffected by the retreat in crude oil.Although energy prices corrected sharply following the easing of geopolitical tensions, tightening import and local availability and expectations of higher replacement costs continued to underpin PP and PE. Meanwhile, PVC lagged due to comfortable supply inside and waning demand, capping more visible hikes. Sellers maintained firm pricing ideas and prepared for further increases in August or even in September, while buyers remained cautious, particularly for distant cargos without exerting significant downward pressure on prices. Indeed, both were stuck between higher upstream costs compared to late June lows and a foggy downstream demand outlook. Unlike China, Türkiye’s market continued to derive its strength primarily from tightening supply conditions for select products, allowing bullish sentiment to survive despite lower crude prices.India: Producer-led rally continues despite comfortable supply India’s domestic PE, PP and PVC markets also maintained their upward trajectory despite the correction in crude oil.Domestic producers continued to implement successive price increases, citing higher upstream costs and tighter replacement economics. PVC recorded the strongest gains, supported further by the implementation of the Minimum Import Price (MIP) policy.At the same time, comfortable supply conditions, transit cargoes and ongoing imports continued to temper buyer enthusiasm. The latest rally therefore remains largely producer-led rather than demand-driven.Whether these higher prices can be sustained will largely depend on post-monsoon demand, which will need to absorb existing inventories and incoming import volumes.Egypt: Market bulls shrug off large oil swingsThe market also remained broadly resilient despite crude oil’s sharp reversal. Higher replacement costs and expectations of firmer August import offers continued to support PE, PP and PVC sentiment, while local producers were expected to seek higher prices. Nevertheless, subdued demand and buyer caution over volatile upstream markets kept trading activity limited, suggesting that cost support outweighed any negative impact from oil’s late-month decline.Regional fundamentals prove stronger than oil volatilityThe late-July collapse in crude oil prices tested the strength of polymer markets worldwide, but its impact varied considerably from one region to another.Europe, Southeast Asia, Türkiye and India largely preserved their firmer tone despite the sharp correction, as supply conditions, replacement costs and producer discipline continued to support prices.China, by contrast, saw its recent rally lose momentum almost immediately after upstream sentiment weakened, highlighting the market’s continued reliance on cost support in the absence of stronger demand.The contrasting regional responses suggest that while oil remains an important catalyst for short-term sentiment, market fundamentals continue to determine whether price rallies can withstand periods of heightened energy volatility. ... in just 6 weeks; what happens next? - Cost of Middle East war for Türkiye: Polymer markets surge to 2021–2022 highs, PE exceeds pandemic-peaks -

headline: Fire at German BP refinery; INEOS declares force majeure on phenol and acetone and implements sales allocation mechanism - ChemNet
summary_text: In mid-July 2026, a fire broke out at a BP refinery in Germany. The cut-off of upstream benzene feedstock forced INEOS Phenol, a global leading phenol & acetone producer, to declare force majeure on phenol and acetone and implement allocation quotas for all customers. ... . The Gelsenkirchen BP refinery is the core feedstock supplier for INEOS’European industrial chain: benzene supplied by BP is transported to INEOS’cumene plant in Marl, Germany, and the cumene intermediate is then shipped to the Gladbeck facility for cracking to produce phenol and acetone. ... Faced with unguaranteed raw material supply, INEOS Phenol officially issued a notice declaring force majeure on European phenol and acetone products, and simultaneously rolled out a sales quota allocation system that proportionally cuts deliveries to all customers while prioritizing basic rigid demand orders. As of July 27, 2026, the force majeure declaration and supply quota policy remain in effect. The company has not released a definitive timeline for the resumption of normal deliveries, as restart progress is fully tied to the repair and commissioning schedule of BP’s Gelsenkirchen complex. ... In June 2026, INEOS confirmed it would extend the operation cycle of the Gladbeck plant beyond 2027 while delaying the restart of its idle plant in Dour, Antwerp, Belgium. This concentrated European phenol & acetone supply capacity heavily in Gladbeck, magnifying the shock of the shutdown—there are virtually no alternative production capacities in Europe to offset the supply gap. ... The European phenol & acetone sector has been under sustained pressure from 2025 through 2026: persistently high natural gas and electricity costs, rising EU carbon emission tariffs have lifted overall production costs, while low-cost import cargoes from Asia have undercut domestic regional market prices. ... Multiple European chemical operators have voluntarily reduced operating rates or shut down phenol & acetone capacities. In early 2026, Germany’s Domo Chemical permanently exited the phenol market after its Leuna plant filed for bankruptcy, further contracting effective regional capacity. Acetone prices had already maintained an upward trajectory prior to the fire and force majeure announcement. With no spare inventory or idle capacity buffer available across Europe, spot market tightness escalated rapidly after the incident. ... January–March: Sharp rally from low levels. Downstream buyers stepped up restocking ahead of the Lunar New Year holiday, paired with climbing pure benzene feedstock costs and bullish sentiment driven by geopolitical disruptions, pushing prices steadily higher to a yearly peak of RMB 11,000/ton on March 9. The average first-half price stood at RMB 7,652/ton, rising 6.2% year-on-year and 18.51% quarter-on-quarter versus H2 2025, with an overall price swing of nearly 94% reflecting drastically amplified market volatility. ... April–June: Pullback after the rally. Mid-to-Late July: Renewed upward momentum fueled by European force majeure. The unfolding European supply chain crisis boosted bullish sentiment among domestic traders. East China spot phenol was quoted at RMB 8,200–8,250/ton on July 23, up RMB 100/ton from mid-July, with average weekly prices edging higher; the European supply crunch became the dominant bullish driver for phenol in July. ...
