headline: The Swedish Food Agency is reducing the regulatory burden for food businesses - Setterwalls
summary_text: The Swedish Food Agency is reducing the regulatory burden for food businesses - Setterwalls ... Over the past two years, the Swedish Food Agency has been conducting a comprehensive simplification initiative that aims to reduce the regulatory burden and administrative costs for food businesses in Sweden. The overarching objective has been to draft regulations that take profitability, competitiveness and sustainable transition into account, and to ensure that businesses also are provided with service, clear information and the right support at the right time. This is an ambitious goal. In March 2026, the Swedish Food Agency published its final report, which sets out the results of more than 40 activities carried out. These include regulatory simplification, improved service and efforts to ensure more risk-based controls. ... The Swedish Food Agency’s simplification measures have largely focused on making the regulatory framework more fit for purpose, facilitating compliance for food businesses by issuing new regulations, amending existing ones, and reviewing and updating guidelines for how the regulations are to be interpreted and applied in practice. Examples of these measures are listed and summarised below. ... Furthermore, in 2025, the Swedish Food Agency adopted four new regulations on honey, fruit juice, jam and preserved milk, implementing amended EU directives. These regulations introduce new possibilities regarding permitted processing methods, product names and labelling, and will enter into force on 14 June 2026. ... As of 1 January 2026, the requirement for food businesses to notify the Swedish Food Agency before launching pre-packaged ‘free from’ foods on the Swedish market has been abolished. Under the previous rules, such businesses were obliged to submit notification to the Agency, which in turn forwarded this to the competent control authority without conducting any substantive assessment of the products concerned. Eliminating this obligation means one less administrative step, thereby reducing the regulatory burden and associated costs for affected businesses. ... The Swedish Food Agency also decided in 2024 to amend the regulations (LIVSFS 2006:12) on frozen foods. The amendment means that it is no longer necessary to provide information on the storage temperature and the type of storage equipment required for the frozen food, which simplifies labelling for businesses. ... been expanded. Since 2021, EU rules have permitted on-farm ... The Swedish Food Agency has also changed its interpretation of the rules regarding the labelling of hard cheese as “lactose-free”. All hard cheese is lactose-free, and the Agency has therefore previously regarded such labelling as misleading to the consumer. In 2025, the Agency reviewed and amended its interpretation to allow hard cheese to be labelled as lactose-free. Other neighbouring EU countries, such as Denmark and Germany, already permitted such labelling, and the Agency wished to promote a uniform interpretation within the EU. The amended interpretation is expected to benefit Swedish cheese producers and strengthen the position of domestically produced hard cheese, as well as facilitate matters for international companies selling their goods in several EU countries, which would otherwise risk additional work and increased costs due to differing interpretations among Member States. ... Furthermore, in the spring of 2025, the Swedish Food Agency issued a new policy on processing wild game at approved facilities. This means that businesses with an approved food facility may carry out what are known as processing activities whereby hunters supply wild game or meat for processing and then receive the finished product for consumption in their own households. However, companies must first submit notification to the Swedish Food Agency to ensure that the activity is included in the establishment’s permit and thus subject to Agency supervision. ... Alongside regulatory changes, the Swedish Food Agency has also focused on improving the service it provides to businesses. The Agency’s customer service function has been developed to prioritise business enquiries, and an AI-based chat function is planned for 2026 in order to provide even more rapid responses. The Agency is also developing an AI assistant, which will provide businesses with tailored information on regulations and risks within the food sector. ... The Swedish Food Agency has also taken a number of additional measures aimed at providing a high level of service. The Märk rätt (Correctly Labelled) initiative has produced short training videos on rules for labelling and information on food, aimed primarily at small and start-up businesses. The Swedish Food Agency is also working to streamline export approvals with countries outside the EU/EEA, with this work including opening up markets to export egg products to Vietnam and fresh beef to the Philippines in 2025. When it comes to slaughter planning, administration has been reduced through pre-filled forms and simplified change procedures. ... In 2024, the Swedish Food Agency introduced a new risk classification model. Under the new model, the frequency of inspections is tailored to the actual risk posed by, or existing in, the relevant business. Businesses with a high level of compliance or certification to an approved standard receive fewer inspection visits. This change lies behind the substantial reduction in both the number of inspections and the inspection fees paid by businesses. ... The largest reduction in the number of inspections has occurred at the final stage of the food chain – shops, restaurants and other businesses that supply food directly to consumers – where the number of planned inspections fell by an estimated 32 per cent between 2023 and 2024. At earlier stages, such as dairies, bakeries and wholesalers, inspections fell by around 8 per cent. The model is set to be evaluated in 2026. ... The Swedish Food Agency is also developing a digital solution for remote meat inspection, where pre- and post-slaughter inspections can be carried out via video in real time instead of requiring a veterinarian to be physically present. The change requires amendments to EU legislation but is expected to benefit small slaughterhouses and facilities in rural areas in particular, if and when it is implemented. ... The Swedish Food Agency’s simplification initiative is expected to entail several positive effects for food businesses. New and amended regulations aim to reduce the administrative burden and open up new business opportunities. The new risk classification model has, according to the Agency, led to approximately 22 per cent fewer official inspections for the roughly 95,000 businesses concerned, and companies’ costs for food inspections correspondingly fell by SEK 72 million between 2023 and 2024. Initiatives in service and customer relations are also expected to provide businesses with better support and clearer communication from the Agency. However, the Swedish Food Agency emphasises that it is too early to draw definitive conclusions and that systematic follow-up is planned for 2026. ... The Swedish Food Agency has also made the somewhat cautious assessment that strategic EU work will have the greatest impact in the long term. The Agency has therefore submitted proposals to the government, including more innovation-friendly rules, a more stable regulatory framework with reasonable transition periods, and better impact assessments. Key areas highlighted include mandatory labelling of alcoholic beverages, simplifications to drinking water regulations, removal of the reference number requirement for unpackaged beef, and updating of regulations for baby food and cereal-based foods. The Agency has also presented an action plan for its ongoing work, focusing on effective regulations, efficient service, dialogue with businesses, and risk-based and consistent controls.

headline: Sugar cane farmers take fight to Treasury as imports surge

headline: Fiji approves private sugar imports to bolster supply as 2026 harvest begins - FijiGlobalNews
summary_text: Fiji approves private sugar imports to bolster supply as 2026 harvest begins - FijiGlobalNews ... # Fiji approves private sugar imports to bolster supply as 2026 harvest begins ... The Government has given private businesses permission to import refined sugar to shore up domestic supplies after shoppers and retailers reported thin or empty supermarket shelves, Finance Minister Esrom Immanuel said in Nadi yesterday. While the Ministry of Agriculture and the Sugar Industry has found some stocks to be “sufficient,” Immanuel said the import option was approved to guard against an expected shortfall ahead of local production picking up. ... “We had checked last week. The Ministry of Agriculture and Sugar Industry had mentioned there is some sufficient stock,” Immanuel told reporters. “But we have allowed businesses, if they can import sugar as well because it will cater for the expected shortage. However … the 2026 harvesting season has already started and that probably can cater for sugar supply in the next two to three months.” The minister indicated the move is aimed at meeting immediate consumer demand while the new crop comes through. ... Retailers and consumers across Fiji have been raising the alarm about low sugar availability in recent days, prompting the government’s swift response. Under the new permission, any licensed importer or business will be able to bring in sugar from overseas markets to supply supermarkets and other outlets until local production stabilises. ... Labasa cane farmer and Minister for Multi‑Ethnic Affairs Charan Jeath Singh warned the relief measure carries risks for the domestic industry if managed poorly. “It’s much cheaper to import and sell than what it costs to produce sugar locally,” Singh said, urging caution so that imports do not undercut farmers and processors. “Let’s not kill this industry … Sugar industry is very competitive in the global market. It needs economics of scale to survive,” he added, echoing long‑running concerns about the sector’s competitiveness against cheaper international sugar. ... Fiji already sources imported sugar from countries including Indonesia, New Zealand, Australia, Malaysia and Thailand. The decision to allow broader private imports comes against a backdrop of production disruptions last year, including the Rarawai Mill fire in September 2025 and a tight harvesting window reported in October 2025 that left significant cane still to be collected. Those events exacerbated seasonal supply gaps and contributed to worries about retail availability ahead of the 2026 harvest. ... The Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC), which plays a central role in domestic processing and supply, did not comment. FSC chief executive officer Bhan Pratap Singh declined calls seeking a response yesterday. The Ministry of Agriculture and the Sugar Industry has not yet outlined any conditions or monitoring arrangements for the private imports beyond the initial approval announced by the Finance Minister. ... With the 2026 crush now under way, authorities are betting that increased milling output will relieve pressure within two to three months. In the meantime, allowing imports aims to prevent immediate disruptions to households and businesses, even as industry figures caution that prolonged reliance on cheaper foreign sugar could further squeeze Fiji’s cane farmers and processors.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka will lead a two-day round of consultations across Fiji’s cane belt starting today, heading a parliamentary Special Committee on the Sugar Industry to hear directly from farmers, mill operators and other stakeholders about the future of the sector. The consultations, organised by the Ministry of Agriculture, Waterways and Sugar Industry, will visit Rakiraki, Ba, Lautoka and Lomawai over the two-day program. ... The committee will open in Rakiraki this morning before travelling to Ba for a tour of the Rarawai Sugar Mill and a meeting with farmers from the Ba mill area at the Ba Civic Centre. On the second day the delegation will convene industry institutions and stakeholders at the Fiji Sugar Corporation’s Training Centre in Lautoka, follow with consultations with sugarcane farmers and a tour of the Lautoka Sugar Mill, and conclude with a final farmers’ meeting in Lomawai before returning to Suva. ... Rabuka chairs the Special Committee on the Sugar Industry, which features a crossbench of senior parliamentarians and ministers: Professor Biman Prasad, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Tourism and Civil Aviation Viliame Gavoka, Manoa Kamikamica, Minister for Sugar Tomasi Tunabuna, Minister for Policing Ioane Naivalurua, Leader of the Opposition Inia Seruiratu, and an opposition-nominated representative. The presence of Cabinet ministers alongside opposition figures signals the government’s intent to collect a broad range of views as it shapes policy responses for the sector. ... In September government ministers confirmed temporary relief measures and a $15-per-tonne compensation for cane redirected to Lautoka after a fire disrupted operations at the Rarawai Mill in Ba. Earlier relief programs this season also targeted farmers affected by pre‑season burnt cane and other losses, while local producers have raised long‑running concerns including land salinity, mill infrastructure, transport logistics and farm viability. ... Organisers say the face‑to‑face meetings will allow cane farmers and industry stakeholders to raise immediate concerns — from compensation and harvest arrangements to long‑term issues such as land rehabilitation and mill capacity — and to contribute ideas to strengthen the sector’s sustainability and productivity. The tour’s mix of mill visits and community consultations is intended to give committee members first‑hand appreciation of both processing bottlenecks and on‑farm challenges. ... Prime Minister Rabuka’s active leadership of the Special Committee is the latest development in a sequence of government interventions aimed at keeping this season’s harvest on track and addressing the structural problems that have dogged the industry for years. How the committee’s findings will be translated into specific policy measures or funding commitments has not been announced; the consultations are expected to inform the committee’s subsequent work in Parliament and any formal recommendations to Cabinet. ... Farmers and stakeholders attending the meetings in Rakiraki, Ba, Lautoka and Lomawai will have an opportunity to present their views directly to senior decision‑makers over the two days, with organisers stressing the engagement is meant to feed practical solutions into the government’s planning for the sugar season and beyond.
